en: Abhidharmasamuccaya: Homage to the Buddha. [Now, within the Fundamental Section, the first chapter: The Investigation of the Three Dharmas.]
In the [section on] characteristics, there is the compendium of the three dharmas, their association, and their classification;
in the [section on] ascertainment, there are the truths, the dharmas, attainment, and discussion.

How many [clinging-aggregates] are there? From what [do they arise]? What is their appropriation? Their establishment and their characteristics; as well as their sequence, purpose, examples, and divisions—these are to be known in the compendium.
How many are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas)? There are five aggregates:

the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāraskandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).

The elements are eighteen: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

There are twelve sense bases: the eye base, the form base, the ear base, the sound base, the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the taste base, the body base, the tangible-base, the mind base,
and the mental-object base.
On what basis are there exactly five aggregates?
On the basis of manifesting the fivefold entities of the self:

the entity of the self as the body together with its possessions, the entity of the self as enjoyment, the entity of the self as verbal expression, and the entity of the self as the formative activity of all dharmas and non-dharmas. (Abhidh-s 2)
And it is also based upon the self-substance that serves as its support.
On what basis are there exactly eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
On the basis of their maintaining the past and present sixfold modes of experience through two types of appropriation: that of the body and that of the objects of enjoyment.
On what basis are there exactly twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*)?
On the basis of their being the gateways for the future sixfold experience through two types of appropriation: the appropriation of the body and the appropriation of objects.
Why are the aggregates (skandhas) called "clinging" (upādāna)?
Because they are accompanied by clinging, the aggregates are called "clinging.
What is clinging?
There is desire and passion for the aggregates.
Why?
Because desire and passion are called "clinging."
Because they bring about the future and present aggregates and because they do not abandon them;
and because there is longing for the future and attachment to the present, desire (*chanda*) and greed (*rāga*) are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Why are the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) said to be phenomena associated with clinging (*sopādāna*)?
In that regard, the exposition is like that of the aggregates.
What is the characteristic of form?
Form has the characteristic of being affected (rūpaṇa).
It is of two kinds.
There is deformation by contact and deformation by location.
What is deformation by contact?
It is the affliction caused by contact with hands, feet, stones, weapons, staffs, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, and so forth.

What is the deformation by location? It is the deformation by place, characterized by the mental attention to a reflected image through directed or undirected mental discursive thought (*vitarka*), thinking: "This and that is form; it is form in such and such a way."
What is the characteristic of feeling?
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing.
It is called "experience" because by means of it, one experiences the ripening of the fruits of various kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
What is the characteristic of perception?
Perception has the characteristic of perceiving;
perception has as its intrinsic nature the grasping of the reflected images of various phenomena.
That by which one engages with objects that have been seen, heard, thought, and known.
What is the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
Conditioned phenomena have the characteristic of volitional formation (*abhisaṃskāra*); their intrinsic nature is the volitional formation of conditioned phenomena.
That by which one directs the mind toward the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate—
what is the characteristic of consciousness? Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
Consciousness is that by which one cognizes various objects, namely forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What is the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
That eye by which one has seen or sees forms, and that accumulated seed of it within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is the eye.
Just as is the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so too are the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.
What is the characteristic of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Form—that which has been seen by the eye and that which is being seen—and wherein the eye-element exercises sovereignty; such is the characteristic of the form-element.
Just as is the characteristic of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), so too are the characteristics of the sound-, odor-, taste-, touch-, and mental-object-elements (*dharmadhātu*).
What is the characteristic of the eye-consciousness-element?
It is the discernment of form based on the eye and having form as its object, as well as its accumulated seed.
The ripening storehouse-consciousness has the characteristic of that eye-consciousness element.
Just as is the characteristic of the visual consciousness element, so too are the characteristics of the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements.
What is the characteristic of the sense-field (*āyatana*)?
It should be understood according to its application, just like the element (*dhātu*).
What is the definition of the aggregate of form?
Whatever is form, all that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is the earth element? It is solidity.
What is the water element? It is fluidity.
What is the fire element?
It is heat.
What is the wind element? It is the state of motion.
What is derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*)?

It is the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty; a portion of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; and the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the eye faculty?
Derived from the four great elements, it is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
What is the auditory faculty?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness, derived from the four great elements.
What is the olfactory faculty?
Derived from the four great elements, it is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness.
What is the tongue faculty?
It is the translucent matter that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness, derived from the four great elements.
What is the body faculty?
It is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for body-consciousness.
What is form?
It is the object within the range of the visual faculty, derived from the four great elements;
such as blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, subtle, high, low, even, uneven, sunlight, shadow, light, darkness, and cloud.
Smoke, dust, and mist;
visible form in open space; informative form; and the uniform color of the sky are [the types of] form.
Furthermore, that is threefold:
beautiful, ugly, and that which is contrary to both.
What is sound?
It is an object derived from the four great elements that is apprehended by the auditory faculty;
it may be pleasant, unpleasant, or neither of these two.

What is odor? It is that which has as its cause either appropriated great elements, or unappropriated great elements, or both; it is either well-known in the world, or brought forth by accomplished beings (*siddha*), or imagined, or taught by the Noble Ones, or taught by non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). What is odor?
It is an object derived from the four great elements that is apprehended by the olfactory faculty;
for example, pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, neutral fragrance, innate fragrance, combined fragrance, and transformed fragrance.
What is taste?
It is the object apprehended by the tongue-faculty, derived from the four great elements;
it is bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and astringent.
Whether it be agreeable, disagreeable, or neither of the two; whether innate, produced by combination, or resulting from transformation.
What is the portion of the tangible?
It is the object apprehended by the body-faculty, derived from the four great elements; namely:
smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, sliminess, slackness, non-slackness, coldness, and heat.
Hunger, thirst, satiety, strength, weakness, fainting, itching, putrefaction, disease, old age, death, fatigue, rest, and vigor.
What is form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
It is fivefold:
that which is contracted, that which is spatial, that which is undertaken, that which is imagined, and that which is derived from mastery.
What is the definition of the aggregate of feeling?
It consists of the six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
In this way, there are six bodies of feeling: pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

Furthermore, there is pleasant bodily feeling, painful bodily feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily feeling; pleasant mental feeling, painful mental feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feeling; pleasant worldly feeling, painful worldly feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant worldly feeling; and pleasant unworldly feeling, painful unworldly feeling.

Furthermore, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is non-sensual; pleasant feeling based on attachment is painful; pleasant feeling based on renunciation is neither-painful-nor-pleasant; painful feeling based on attachment is painful; and painful feeling based on renunciation is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
What is bodily feeling?
It is feeling associated with the five consciousnesses.
What is mental feeling?
It is feeling associated with the mental consciousness.
What is worldly feeling?
Feeling associated with craving for personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
What is non-materialistic feeling?
Feeling dissociated from that craving.
What is sensation based on greed? It is sensation associated with craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
What is sensation based on renunciation?
It is sensation dissociated from craving for that [sensation]. What is the formal definition of the aggregate of perception?
There are six groups of perception:
perception born of eye-contact,
and [perception born of] ear, nose, [tongue, body, and mind-contact].

Perception born of tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact perceives as having a sign (*sanimitta*), and also perceives as signless (*animitta*); it perceives as limited (*parītta*), as extensive (*mahadgata*), as immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and even as "there is nothing" (*na kiṃcid asti*), which is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
What is the perception with signs (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*)?

It is any perception other than those of one unskilled in conventional expression, of one who has attained the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), and of one who has attained the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), setting aside [those specific] perceptions.
What is the perception of the signless? It is that perception which has been set aside.
What is limited perception?
It is that by which one perceives the realm of desire.
What is the perception of vastness?
It is that by which one perceives the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
What is the perception of the immeasurable?
It is that by which one perceives the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
What is the perception of nothingness?
It is that by which one perceives the sphere of nothingness.
What is the definition of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)?
It consists of the six groups of volition (*cetanākāya*):
volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—by means of which one acts for the sake of wholesomeness.

It intends toward defilement, it intends toward the differentiation of states; this volition, with the exception of feeling and perception, along with other mental factors and formations dissociated from mind, is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

What, then, are they? They are: attention, contact, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, shame, dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, vigor, serenity, heedfulness, equanimity, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance.

Doubt, the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes, the esteeming of views, the esteeming of rules and rituals, false view, anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, avarice, deceit, arrogance, harmfulness, lack of shame,
lack of embarrassment, lethargy, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, negligence, forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and distraction.
Drowsiness, regret, applied thought, and sustained thought.
What is volition (*cetanā*)? It is the mental formation (*abhisaṃskāra*) that is the action of the mind; its function is to impel the mind toward what is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is attention? It is the mental application of the mind;
its function is to sustain the mind upon the object.
What is contact?
It is the discernment of the modification of the sense faculty upon the coming together of the three.
Its function is to provide a basis for feeling.
What is desire (*cchanda*)? It is the wish to act directed toward a desired object, brought about by this or that [cause]. Its function is to provide a basis for the undertaking of vigor (*vīrya*).
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)? It is the holding fast to a determined object according to that determination. Its function is to be unshakable.
What is mindfulness? It is the non-forgetting of a familiar object by the mind, having the function of non-distraction.
What is concentration? It is one-pointedness of mind upon an object to be examined;
its function is to provide a basis for knowledge.
What is wisdom?
It is the discernment of phenomena with respect to the very object under investigation;
its function is the removal of doubt.
What is faith (*śraddhā*)?
It is conviction, clarity, and aspiration regarding existence, virtue, and capacity.
Its function is to provide a basis for desire (*chanda*).
What is *hrī*? It is shame regarding one's own faults;
its function is to provide a basis for the restraint of misconduct.
What is shame (*apatrāpya*)? It is the feeling of embarrassment regarding one's faults in relation to others;
its function is precisely that.
What is non-attachment (*alobha*)? It is the absence of clinging toward existence or the requisites for existence; its function is to provide a basis for the non-engagement in misconduct.
What is non-hatred (*adveṣa*)?
Non-malice toward sentient beings and toward phenomena that are suffering or conducive to suffering;
its function is to provide a basis for the non-engagement in misconduct.
What is non-delusion?
Discrimination (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is knowledge by way of maturation, scripture, or realization;
its function is to provide a basis for the non-occurrence of misconduct.
What is vigor (*vīrya*)?
Vigor of the mind toward the wholesome consists of enthusiasm for armor, or for application, or for non-depression, or for non-retrogression, or for non-contentment;
its function is the fulfillment and perfection of the side of the wholesome.
What is serenity (*praśrabdhi*)? It is the serviceability of body and mind resulting from the subsiding of the dysfunctions of body and mind;
its function is to extract all hindrances.
What is non-intoxication (*amadamada*)?
It is the cultivation of wholesome factors based on diligence, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as the protection of the mind against tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
Its function is the fulfillment and perfection of mundane and supramundane prosperity.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It is that evenness of mind, composure of mind, and state of mental non-exertion which, relying on energy along with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, is opposed to dwelling in affliction;
its function is to provide a basis that allows no opportunity for affliction.
What is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)? It is a mental state characterized by non-aversion, which is compassion; its function is to refrain from injury.
What is attachment? It is the craving belonging to the three realms;
its function is the production of suffering.
What is hostility (*pratigha*)?
It is malice toward sentient beings, toward suffering, and toward those phenomena that are conducive to suffering.
Its function is to provide a basis for dwelling in discomfort and for engaging in misconduct.
What is pride? It is the inflation of the mind based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Its function is to provide a basis for disrespect and the arising of suffering.
What is ignorance?
It is non-knowledge regarding the three realms.
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of afflictions through false certainties and doubt concerning phenomena.
What is doubt? It is indecision regarding the truths;
its function is to provide a basis for the non-engagement in the side of the wholesome.

What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)? It is the acceptance, preference, opinion, examination, and view of one who regards the five aggregates of clinging as a self or as belonging to a self. Its function is to provide a basis for all types of views.
What is the view of grasping at extremes?
It is the acceptance, preference, opinion, examination, and view of one who regards the five aggregates of clinging as either eternal or subject to annihilation.
The middle way has the function of removing obstacles to liberation.

What is adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? It is the acceptance, preference, opinion, examination, and view of one who regards a [false] view and the five aggregates of clinging that serve as the basis for that view as foremost, supreme, distinguished, and preeminent. Its function is to provide a basis for the stubborn attachment to incorrect views.

What is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? It is the acceptance, preference, opinion, examination, and view of one who regards morality, vows, and the five aggregates of clinging that serve as the basis for those moralities and vows as being purity, liberation, and the means of deliverance.
Its function is to provide a basis for the fruitlessness of one's efforts.

What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? It is the acceptance, preference, opinion, examination, and view of one who either denies the cause, the fruit, or the action; or who destroys an existing reality; or who falsely conceptualizes. Its function is the total severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
Its function is to provide a basis for the firmness of the unwholesome roots;
its activity consists in proceeding toward the unwholesome and not proceeding toward the wholesome.
Among these five views, how many are views of superimposition (*samāropa-dṛṣṭi*) and how many are views of negation (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*)?

Four are views of superimposition, based on the superimposition of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) upon the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and based on the superimposition of excellence (*agra*) and purity (*śuddhi*) upon [wrong] views. One is for the most part a view of negation.
And as for those views that speculate about the past and those views that speculate about the future, from how many [of the] views are they to be understood?
From two, or from all.
From how many views should those views regarding indeterminate things be understood?
From two, or from all of them.
Seeing what fault did the Blessed One reject a self within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases by means of five reasons?

One perceives five faults embraced by the view of a self-identity: the fault of having distinct characteristics, the fault of impermanence, the fault of lack of well-being, the fault of being bodiless, and the fault of liberation occurring without effort.

Regarding the twenty-fold view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the five aggregates of clinging: one regards form as the self, the self as possessing form, form as belonging to the self, or the self as being in form; likewise, one regards feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, the self as possessing consciousness, consciousness as belonging to the self, or the self as being in consciousness. Among these, how many are views of a self and how many are views of what belongs to a self? There are five views of a self.
There are fifteen views regarding what belongs to a self.

For what reason are there five views of "mine"? It is by way of taking possession through connection, taking possession through exercising control, and taking possession through inseparable functioning.
Should the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) be said to have a determined object-base, or should it be said to have an undetermined object-base?
It should be described as having an unascertained object, like the cognition of a snake in a rope. What is anger?
When a cause for harm is present, resentment (*cetasa āghāta*) belonging to the category of hostility (*pratighāṃśika*) arises;
its function is to provide a basis for the fury of taking up weapons, taking up sticks, and so forth.
What is enmity (*upanāha*)? It is that which follows thereafter, belonging to the same category of hostility, consisting in the non-relinquishing of the intent for vengeance.
Its function is to provide a basis for non-forbearance.
What is concealment (*mrakṣa*)? It is the hiding of one's faults by one who has been correctly exhorted, and it belongs to the category of delusion (*moha*).
Its function is to provide a basis for dwelling in remorse and discomfort. What is envy (*mātsarya*)?
It is a form of mental hostility belonging to the category of aversion (*pratighāṃśika*), preceded by anger and resentment.
Its function is to provide a basis for loud, intense, and harsh speech; its function is to produce demerit; and its function is to result in an unpleasant state of existence.
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? It is a mental resentment, belonging to the portion of hatred, produced by intolerance toward the excellence of another's prosperity in one who is attached to gain and honor;
its function is to dwell in a state of dejection and lack of ease.

What is avarice? It is the mind’s grasping at requisites, characterized by a portion of attachment, in one who is obsessed with gain and honor; its function is to provide a basis for the lack of austerity.

What is deceit (*māyā*)? It is the manifestation of non-existent qualities by one who is attached to gain and honor; it belongs to the categories of passion and delusion, and its function is to provide a basis for wrong livelihood.
What is deceit (*śāṭhya*)? It is the concealment of actual faults by one who is intent upon gain and honor, and which belongs to the categories of attachment and delusion.
It creates an obstacle to obtaining correct instruction.

What is pride (mada)? It is the joy and mental satisfaction that belongs to the category of attachment, arising from health, youth, the attainment of signs of long life, or any other kind of contaminated prosperity.
Its function is to provide a basis for all primary and secondary afflictions.
What is harmfulness?
It is a state of hostility, lack of compassion, lack of kindness, and lack of mercy;
its function is to cause injury.

What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)? It is a portion of attachment, aversion, and delusion, consisting of a lack of embarrassment regarding one's own faults; its function is to assist all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*).
What is lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*)?
It is a portion of attachment, aversion, and delusion consisting in the absence of shame regarding faults in relation to others;
its function is to assist all primary and secondary afflictions.
What is lethargy (*styāna*)? It is a lack of serviceability of the mind belonging to the portion of delusion; its function is to assist all primary and secondary afflictions.
What is restlessness?
It is the lack of tranquility of the mind belonging to the portion of attachment in one who pursues a beautiful object;
its function is to act as an obstacle to calm abiding (*śamatha*).
What is lack of faith (*āśraddhya*)? It is a portion of delusion; it consists of the mind’s lack of conviction, lack of clarity, and lack of aspiration toward wholesome phenomena.
Its function is to provide a basis for laziness (*kausīdya*).

What is laziness? It is a lack of mental exertion belonging to the portion of delusion, arising from a fondness for sleep, reclining on one's side, and lying down; its function is to act as an obstacle to the application of oneself to the side of wholesome qualities.
What is lack of joy (*pramoda*)?
It is the non-cultivation of wholesome states and the failure to guard the mind against tainted states, based upon attachment, aversion, and delusion accompanied by laziness.
Its function is to provide a basis for the increase of the unwholesome and the decline of the wholesome.
What is forgetfulness?
It is mindfulness associated with the afflictions;
its function is to provide a basis for distraction.
What is lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)?
It is wisdom associated with the afflictions, by means of which the activities of body, speech, and mind proceed without being clearly cognized.
Its function is to provide a basis for transgressions.
What is distraction (*vikṣepa*)? It is the wandering of the mind belonging to the portions of attachment, aversion, and delusion.

Furthermore, it is: distraction by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikṣepa*), outward distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*), inward distraction (*adhyātma-vikṣepa*), and [distraction by way of] signs (*nimitta*...).
Distraction consists of distraction due to corruption and distraction due to mental attention.
What is distraction by nature?
It is the five groups of consciousness.
What is external distraction?
It is the wandering of the mind toward the five strands of sensual pleasure for one who is engaged in the practice of the wholesome.
What is internal distraction?
It is the relishing of lethargy and restlessness in one who is engaged in the wholesome.
What is distraction of signs?
Application to the wholesome by placing esteem for the recognition of others at the forefront.

What is the distraction of depravity (*dauṣṭhulya-vikṣepa*)? It is the grasping, the intermingling, and the taking of signs— such as "I," "mine," or "I am"— which, having arisen from the depravity associated with the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*), "mine" (*mamakāra*), and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), occurs in one engaged in the wholesome regarding each feeling that arises.

What is distraction of attention (*manasikāravikṣepa*)? It is the scattering [of the mind] occurring when one is entering another meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or another vehicle (*yāna*), or by way of taking recourse [to them]. Its function is to act as an obstacle to dispassion (*vairāgya*). What is torpor (*middha*)?

Based on the sign of wealth, it is a contraction of the mind belonging to the portion of delusion; it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; occurring at the proper time or the improper time; appropriate or inappropriate;
and its function is to provide a basis for the failure to accomplish what ought to be done.

What is remorse (*kaukṛtya*)? It is a mental regret that is a part of delusion (*moha*), arising from having performed or not performed what was intended or unintended; it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, and it may occur at the proper time or the improper time, and be appropriate or inappropriate.
Its function is to create obstacles to the stability of the mind.
What is vitarka? It is a mental discourse that investigates, based either on volition or on wisdom;
and it is a coarseness of the mind.
What is investigation (*vicāra*)? It is a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that examines, based either on volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*);
and it is the subtlety of the mind.
Their function is to provide a basis for dwelling in either comfort or discomfort.
Furthermore, the function of wholesome factors is the abandonment of their own opposites;
the function of the afflictions and secondary afflictions is the obstruction of their respective antidotes.
What are the formations dissociated from mind? They are:

acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneity of a group (*nikāyasabhāgatā*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), the sets of phrases (*padakāya*), the sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
Specific determination, conjunction, velocity, sequence, time, place, number, and completeness.
What is acquisition (*prāpti*)? It is a designation for the accumulation and diminution of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; it is termed "acquisition," "attainment," and "possession."
What is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)?

It is the designation for the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors through a mental attention preceded by the perception of liberation, [applied] by one who is free from passion for the Śubhakṛtsna realm but not yet free from passion for what is above it.
What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It is the designation for the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors through a mental attention preceded by the perception of peaceful abiding, in one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and has transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
What is the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika)?
It is the designation for the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors in one who has been reborn among the gods of the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva).
What is the life-faculty? It is the designation "vitality" (āyus) for the determination of the duration of existence within a particular homogeneous class of beings, projected by prior karma.
What is the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga)? It is the designation for the similarity of the personal existence (ātmabhāva) among various sentient beings within their respective classes of beings.
What is birth?
It is the designation for the coming into existence of conditioned phenomena, having previously not existed, within a homogeneous class of beings.
What is aging?
It is the designation "aging" for the alteration of the continuity of conditioned phenomena within a homogeneous class.
What is duration?
It is the designation for the non-disappearance of the continuity within a homogeneous class of beings.
What is impermanence?
It is the designation "impermanence" for the destruction of the continuity of conditioned phenomena within a homogeneous class of beings.
What are the sets of names?
The designation "sets of names" refers to the verbal expressions for the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
What are the sets of phrases?
The designation "sets of phrases" refers to the specific designations for phenomena.

What are the sets of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)? They are designated as "sets of phonemes" with respect to the syllables that serve as the basis for both [nouns and verbs], on account of their manifesting both of those. They are also called "letters" (*varṇa*).
It is based on the thorough elucidation of the meaning;
furthermore, it is based on the non-decay of the syllables as alternative expressions.
What is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)? It is the designation for the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
What is "occurrence"?
It is the designation for the non-interruption of the continuity of cause and fruit.
What is "specific determination"?
The designation "specific determination" refers to the distinctness of cause and fruit.
What is yoga?
It is the designation "yoga" for the correspondence between cause and fruit.
What is speed?
It is the designation "speed" applied to the rapid occurrence of cause and effect.
What is succession?
It is the designation "succession" with respect to the proceeding of causes and effects one after another.
What is time?
Time is a designation for the continuous progression of the causal series of cause and effect.
What is space?
Space is a designation for the cause and effect themselves in all ten directions—east, south, west, north, below, above, and everywhere.
What is number?
It is the designation "number" applied to the individual distinctions among conditioned phenomena.
What is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? It is the designation "causal complex" applied to the convergence of causes, fruits, and conditions. 0.
What is the definition of the aggregate of consciousness?
It is that which is mind (*citta*) and also mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In this regard: (Abhidh-s 12)
What is the mind (*citta*)?

It is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is permeated by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and contains all seeds; it is also the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the appropriating-consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), based on the accumulation of those very latencies.
What is the *manas*?

It is the *ālayavijñāna* which, at all times, has the nature of mentation and is associated with four afflictions: the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), attachment to self (*ātmasneha*), the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is omnipresent, whether in the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the neutral—excepting the manifestation of the Path (*mārgasammukhībhāva*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣabhūmi*)—and that which [is present] in the six consciousnesses...
Consciousness that has just ceased.
What is consciousness?
It consists of the six groups of consciousness:
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
What is eye-consciousness?
It is the representation based on the eye and having visible form as its object.
What is auditory consciousness?
It is the specific cognition that has the ear as its basis and sound as its object.
What is olfactory consciousness?
It is the representation based on the nose and having odor as its object. What is gustatory consciousness?
It is the specific cognition based on the tongue and having taste as its object.
What is body-consciousness?
It is the discernment that has the body as its basis and tangible objects as its object.
What is mental consciousness?
It is the discernment that has the mind as its support and mental phenomena as its object.
What is the formal establishment of the elements (*dhātu*)?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) itself consists of ten elements:

the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*), the form element (*rūpadhātu*), the ear element (*śrotradhātu*), the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the tongue element (*jivhādhātu*), the taste element (*rasadhātu*), the body element (*kāyadhātu*), the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), and a portion of the mind element (*manodhātu*).
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations constitute a portion of the dharma-element.
The aggregate of consciousness itself constitutes the seven consciousness-elements:
the six consciousness-elements beginning with the eye-consciousness, and the mind-element.
What within the dharma-realm is not included among the aggregates? Within the dharma-realm, these are the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, those unconditioned phenomena are of eight kinds.

The suchness of wholesome phenomena, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena, the suchness of indeterminate phenomena, space, non-analytical cessation, analytical cessation, the imperturbable, and the cessation of perception and feeling— among these, what is the suchness of wholesome phenomena?
It is selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Furthermore, it is called emptiness, the signless, the limit of reality, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena.
On what basis is suchness called "suchness"?
On the basis of its being non-otherwise.
On what basis is suchness called "selflessness"?
Based on its dissociation from the two kinds of self.
Based on what is suchness called emptiness?
Based on the non-occurrence of all afflictions.
(Abhidh-s 13) On what basis is suchness called "signless"?
On the basis of the subsiding of all signs.
On what basis is suchness called "the limit of reality"?
Based on its being an object that is free from error.
On what basis is suchness called the ultimate truth?
Based on its being the locus and range of the knowledge of the ultimate truth.
On what basis is suchness called the *dharmadhātu*?
It is on the basis of its being the support for the signs of the Buddha-dharma for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Just as is the suchness of wholesome phenomena, so should the suchness of unwholesome phenomena and the suchness of indeterminate phenomena be understood.
What is space?
It is the absence of form, by virtue of providing room for all activities.
What is analytical cessation? It is that cessation which is not dissociation.
What is analytical cessation?
It is that cessation which is dissociation.
What is the immovable?
It is the cessation of pleasure for one who is free from passion for the sphere of universal purity (śubhakṛtsna), but not yet free from passion for what is above it.
What is the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*)?

It is the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors, as well as some stable ones, belonging to one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and has transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), preceded by the mental attention to the perception of dwelling in peace.
The five forms are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations; these eight, together with the unconditioned phenomena, are thus called the sixteen elements (dhātus).
What is the establishment of the sense bases (āyatanas)?
The ten form-elements are themselves the ten form-bases.
The seven consciousness elements themselves constitute the mind base (*manāyatana*);
the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*) constitutes the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
By this method, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are subsumed within three phenomena:
the aggregate of form, the element of mental objects, and the sense-base of mind.
Regarding what was said— that there is both the eye and the eye-element—
could it be that something is both the eye and the eye-element,
or could it be that something is both the eye-element and the eye?
There may be that which is the eye but not the eye-element,
such as the final eye of an Arhat.
There may be that which is the eye-element but not the eye.
For example, the eye that was not obtained or was lost while in the egg, the embryo (kalala), the vesicle (arvuda), the flesh-mass (peśī), or in the mother’s womb;
or the cause of the eye belonging to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) born in the formless realms (ārūpya)—
such a thing would be the eye, but not the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu).
In the remaining states,
there would be neither the eye nor the eye-element:
namely, for one who has entered the nirvana-realm without remainder, or for a noble one reborn in the formless realms.
Just as it is with the eye and the eye-element, so too should the ear, nose, tongue, and body elements be understood according to their respective correspondences.
Could it be that what is mind is also the mind-element, or could it be that what is the mind-element is also mind?
It could be that there is mind which is not the mind-element.
For example, the final mind of an Arhat may be the mind-element but not the mind; or,
for example, that which is the cause of the mind in one who has entered the attainment of cessation.
It may be that it is both mind and the mind-element,
as in the remaining states;
it may be neither mind nor the mind-element.
Just as in the case of one who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder,
when one is born in that stage, does one see forms of that stage with an eye belonging to that stage?
One sees forms of that stage with an eye belonging to that stage.
Even by means of [vision] belonging to another level:
one born in the desire realm sees forms belonging to the desire realm with an eye belonging to the desire realm;
and one sees even forms belonging to lower levels with an eye belonging to the form realm or a higher level.
Just as one perceives forms with the eye, so too does one perceive sound with the ear.

Just as when born in the desire realm, so too when born in the form realm, one smells odors, tastes flavors, and experiences tangibles belonging to the desire realm by means of the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile organs that belong to the desire realm.
One born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) perceives tangibles belonging to its own level with a body belonging to the realm of form; in that realm, odors and tastes do not exist by their very nature,
because of the absence of desire for informative action (vijñapti) and for nutriment.
By this same principle, there is no consciousness of the nose or the tongue.
One born in the desire realm cognizes phenomena belonging to the three realms as well as the untainted (anāsrava) phenomena by means of a mind belonging to the desire realm.
Just as when one has arisen in the desire realm, so too when one has arisen in the form realm.

One born in the formless realm cognizes, by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm, the phenomena belonging to the formless realm that pertain to its own level as well as those that are untainted;
and by means of an untainted mind, one cognizes the phenomena belonging to the three realms as well as those that are untainted.
On what basis is the sequence of the aggregates established in that way?
On the basis of their being the support for consciousness.
The four bases of consciousness and the consciousnesses themselves are mutually dependent;
as it is with form, so it is with existence;
as one feels, so one perceives.
As one perceives, so one intends;
as one intends, so consciousness becomes directed toward this or that state,
according to the principles of affliction and purification.
Wherein one is afflicted and purified:
through the mental formation of grasping at the signs of feeling, one is afflicted and purified by means of affliction and purification.
By this method, the sequence of the aggregates is explained.
How is the sequence of the elements (dhātu) thus established?
It is based on the occurrence of conceptualization regarding worldly objects.
What is the worldly engagement in the conceptualization of objects?
In the world, one first sees;
having seen, (Abhidh-s 15)
He exchanges [garments];
having exchanged them, he offers perfumes and garlands to the one who has been bathed;
then he serves various kinds of excellent food.
Thereupon, he attends upon many beds, seats, female slaves, and retinues;
furthermore, from the mental element as well, there arise various conceptual constructions regarding those very things.
And thus, following the sequence of the internal element, there is the establishment of the external element;
following that sequence, there is the establishment of the consciousness element.
Just as it is with the sequence of the elements, so it is also with the sense-bases.

What is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha)? Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; whether far or near—all that, taken together, is called the aggregate of form.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is so called in the sense of a heap, like a heap of wealth;
and so it continues up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
Furthermore, it is called a "skandha" on account of its characteristic of being an extensive mass of suffering, just as one speaks of the trunk of a great tree. As it is said in the Sūtra:
Just as from the arising of absolute and great suffering.
Moreover, it is called a "skandha" (aggregate) because it carries the burden by way of affliction,
just as one carries a burden with a shoulder-pole.
What is the meaning of the term "dhātu" (element)?
The meaning of the seed of all phenomena; the meaning of maintaining its own characteristic;
the meaning of maintaining the state of cause and effect.
And for the purpose of collecting and maintaining all types of phenomena.
What is the meaning of "base" (āyatana)? The meaning of a base is the sense of a gateway for consciousness.
As spoken by the Buddha: "Form is like a bubble, feeling is like foam, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion.
For what reason is form said to be like a bubble, up to consciousness being like an illusion?
Because they are without self, impure, of inferior flavor, unstable, and devoid of essence.
(Thus ends the second part of the first chapter on the Three Dharmas within the Fundamental Section.
Furthermore, what are the conceptual distinctions regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases? To this effect, there is a verse of exaltation (*udāna*):
(From the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
16) How, how many, and for what purpose are the substantial entities, the objects of knowledge, the forms, the outflows, the arisen, and so forth, as well as the past and the conditions?

Regarding the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana): how many are substantially existent (dravyasat)? What is the purpose of the investigation into what is substantially existent?
That which is the objective domain of the sense faculties, independent of verbal expression and independent of anything else, is substantially existent.
All [of these] are substantially existent.
For the purpose of abandoning attachment to the substance of a self.
In what sense is something "conceptually designated" (*prajñaptimat*)? How many things are conceptually designated? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is conceptually designated?
That which is the objective domain of the senses, depending upon verbal expression and depending upon something other than itself, is conceptually designated.
Everything is conceptual;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that possesses concepts.
How is it conventional?
How many are conventional?
For what purpose is the investigation of the conventional? That which has defilement as its object is the conventional.
Everything is conventional,
for the purpose of abandoning the self-clinging that is the cause of affliction.
What is ultimate existence?
How many things are ultimately existent? For what purpose is the investigation of ultimate existence undertaken?
The object of purification is ultimate reality;
everything is ultimate reality.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self characterized by the signs of purification.
How is the knowable to be understood? How many things are knowable? For what purpose is the examination of the knowable? There are five knowables:
form, mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned.

In this regard, all that is to be known is based upon: where there is affliction and purification; that which is afflicted or purified; that which causes affliction or brings about purification; and the state therein as well as the nature of purification.

In that context, "form" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the ten form-elements (rūpadhātu), the ten form-bases (rūpāyatana), and those forms included within the element and base of mental objects (dharmadhātvāyatana).
Mind is the aggregate of consciousness, the seven elements of consciousness, and the sense-base of mind.

Mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) consist of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) consist of the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind and a portion of the sphere of phenomena and the sphere of mental objects.
The unconditioned is a portion of the sphere of phenomena and the sphere of mental objects.

Furthermore, objects of knowledge (*jñeya-dharma*) are also to be understood from the perspective of the range of knowledge consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of reasoning (*yukti-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of non-distraction (*avisāra-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of individual self-realization (*pratyātma-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of the cognition of others (*parātma-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of lower [levels] (*adhara-jñāna*), the range of knowledge consisting of higher [levels] (*ūrdhva-jñāna*),
and the range of knowledge consisting of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-jñāna*). (a)

It is for the purpose of eliminating the self-clinging of one who conceives of a knower and a seer, [taught] from the perspective of the domain of knowledge of origination, from the perspective of the domain of knowledge of non-arising, from the perspective of the domain of knowledge of knowledge, from the perspective of the domain of knowledge of culmination, and from the perspective of the domain of knowledge of great purpose.
(Abhidh-s 17) How is the cognizable (*vijñeya*) to be understood? How many are the cognizables? For what purpose is the investigation of the cognizable?

The cognizable is to be viewed from the perspective of non-conceptualization, as well as from conceptualization; from the perspective of cause, as well as from activity; from the perspective of the sign (*nimitta*), as well as from that which possesses the sign (*naimittaka*); from the perspective of the adverse side and its antidote (*vipakṣa-pratipakṣa*), and also from the perspective of subtle distinctions.
All things are to be known for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self as a seer and so forth.
How are they to be directly known? How many are to be directly known? For what purpose is the investigation of those things to be directly known?
They are to be directly known by way of transition, by way of oral tradition, by way of entering into conduct, by way of coming, by way of going, and by way of departure.
All of these are to be directly known.
It is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self endowed with majestic power.
What is the material? How many are material? For what purpose is the investigation of the material?

It is material by way of its own nature, by way of being based on the primary elements (*bhūta*), by way of the arising of delight (*nandī*), by way of locality, by way of pervading space, by way of the teaching of location, by way of the range of location, by way of the range of the two conventions, by way of connection, and by way of continuity.

The material (*rūpin*) should be understood by way of its manifestation, its affliction, its attainment, its establishment through accumulation, its outward orientation, its inward orientation, its extension, its limitation, its temporality,
and its illustration; or else, all material things should be understood according to their respective application.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self consisting of form.
How is it formless? How many are formless? For what purpose is the investigation of the formless?
That which is the opposite of the formed is formless;
all are formless, or they are so according to their respective application.
For the purpose of abandoning the deep-seated attachment to a formless self.
What is the visible? How many are the visibles? For what purpose is the examination of the visible?
That which is the range of the eye is the visible.
The classification of the remainder is like that of form (*rūpa*).
All [objects] are with demonstration, or as appropriate;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a visual self.
What is the non-demonstrable? How many are non-demonstrable? For what purpose is the investigation of the non-demonstrable?
The non-demonstrable should be understood as the opposite of the demonstrable;
all [dharmas] are non-demonstrable, or they are so according to their respective application.

(a) This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is not visible to the eye. How is it with resistance? How many are with resistance? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is with resistance?
Whatever is demonstrable is also with resistance.
Furthermore, that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) should be understood through three reasons:

by way of its nature (*jāti*), by way of accumulation (*upacaya*), and by way of not being processed (*aparikarmakṛta*). Among these, "by way of its nature" means that it obstructs and is obstructed by another.

In that context, "accumulation" refers to that which is larger than an atom. Among those, "unrefined" refers to that form which does not function under the mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, from the standpoint of being a basis for provocation: it is with resistance (*sapratigha*); all [factors] are with resistance, or they are so according to their respective application.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is not omnipresent (*asarvagata*).
What is non-obstructive? How many are non-obstructive? For what purpose is the investigation of the non-obstructive?
Non-obstructive is the opposite of obstructive.
All [dharmas] are non-obstructive, or they are so according to their respective application.
For the purpose of abandoning the deep-seated attachment to a self that is omnipresent.

What is the contaminated (*sāsrava*), how many are contaminated, and for what purpose is the investigation of the contaminated? The contaminated should be understood from five perspectives: by way of its being the essence of outflows (*āsrava*), by way of connection with outflows, by way of the persistence of outflows, by way of conformity to outflows, and by way of being a derivative of outflows. The five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are contaminated; fifteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of three elements and two bases [are also contaminated].
For the purpose of abandoning the adherence to a self associated with the outflows (*āsrava*).
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*), how many are untainted, and for what purpose is the investigation of the untainted?
The untainted is the opposite of the tainted (*sāsrava*).
It consists of the five aggregates not subject to grasping (*anupādānaskandha*) and a portion of three realms and two bases (*āyatana*).

This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is dissociated from the outflows (*āsrava*). How is there conflict? How many types of conflict are there? For what purpose is the investigation of conflict? Conflict arises by depending upon forms of passion, hatred, and delusion, resulting in the taking up of weapons, the taking up of sticks, quarreling, brawling, strife, and disputes.

It should be viewed as a source of conflict (*saraṇa*) by virtue of its identity with that, its connection with that, its bondage to that, its consequence of that, its conformity to that, and its continuity with that.
As many as there are things with outflows (*sāsrava*), so many are sources of conflict.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self associated with conflict.
What is non-contention? How many types of non-contention are there? For what purpose is non-contention investigated? Non-contention is the opposite of contention.
There are as many types of non-contention as there are untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
For the purpose of abandoning the adherence to a self that is dissociated from conflict.

What is "with attachment" (*sāmiṣa*), how many things are with attachment, and for what purpose is the investigation of that which is with attachment? Whatever forms of greed, hatred, and delusion one relies upon to settle into a self-existence (*ātmabhāva*) subject to renewed birth— that [existence] is [considered with attachment] by way of its being the self,
by way of connection to it, by way of bondage to it, by way of its consequence, by way of its conformity, and by way of its continuity.
These too should be seen as being with attachment (*sāmiṣa*).
As many as there are bases of conflict (*saraṇa*), so many are those with attachment.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the clinging to a self associated with attachment.
What is the undefiled? How many are undefiled? For what purpose is the investigation of the undefiled?
The undefiled is the opposite of the defiled.
There are as many undefiled states as there are non-contentious states.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is dissociated from material things.

How is there that which is based on greed? How many things are based on greed? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is based on greed? That form of attachment, aversion, and delusion by resorting to which one becomes intent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure—this should be seen as being based on greed, whether in terms of its own nature, its connection, its cause, its consequence, its conformity, or its lineage.
As many as there are things associated with worldly attachment (*sāmiṣa*), so many are based on greed (*gredha*).
This is for the purpose of abandoning the self-clinging that is joined with greed.
How is it based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*)? How many are based on renunciation? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is based on renunciation?
That which relies on renunciation is the opposite of that which relies on greed.
As many as there are [states] free from worldly desire, so many rely on renunciation;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is dissociated from greed.

What is the conditioned? How many are the conditioned? For what purpose is the investigation of the conditioned? That for which arising is discerned, as well as passing away and the alteration of duration—all that should be seen as conditioned.
All conditioned things [are included], with the exception of one part of the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana*.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the deep-seated attachment to a self that is impermanent.
What is the unconditioned? How many are the unconditioned? For what purpose is the investigation of the unconditioned?
The unconditioned is the opposite of the conditioned;
it is a portion of the dharma-element and the dharma-sphere.
For the purpose of abandoning the persistent attachment to a permanent self:
it should be said that the aggregates, being without appropriation, are conditioned; or should it be said they are unconditioned?
It should be said that they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
For what reason?
Because it is not conditioned by the formative activity of karma and afflictions, it is not conditioned;
because it can be manifested or withdrawn at will, it is not unconditioned.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "These two are the conditioned and the unconditioned."

Therefore, how can it be that by the same sense in which something is conditioned, it is not unconditioned, and by the sense in which it is unconditioned, it is not conditioned? In this regard, the underlying principle should be observed.
What is the mundane? How many are mundane? For what purpose is the investigation of the mundane?
That which is included within the three realms is mundane, as is that which appears as such and is obtained subsequent to the supramundane.
It consists of a portion of the aggregates, fifteen elements, ten bases, and a portion of three elements and two bases.
For the purpose of abandoning attachment to a self and to the world.
What is the supramundane? How many are supramundane? For what purpose is the investigation of the supramundane?
The supramundane is that which is the antidote to the three realms, and it is non-conceptual by virtue of being free from error, free from conceptual proliferation, and non-conceptual.
Furthermore, by way of another formulation, that which is supramundane is also supramundane when obtained subsequent to the supramundane,
based on its reliance upon the supramundane;
it constitutes a portion of the aggregates, three of the elements, and two of the sense-bases.
It is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a solitary self.
(Abhidh-s 20) How is it arisen? How many are arisen? For what purpose is the investigation of the arisen?
That which is past and present is the arisen.
A single portion of all [these] is for the purpose of abandoning the adherence to a non-eternal self.
Furthermore, there are twenty-four kinds of arisen [phenomena]:

arisen at the beginning, arisen as a continuity, arisen through accumulation, arisen as a basis, arisen as a transformation, arisen through maturation, arisen through decline, arisen through distinction, arisen as luminous, arisen as non-luminous, and arisen through transition.

It arises with seeds, it arises without seeds, it arises as a reflection, it arises through mastery, it arises through succession, it arises through momentary disintegration, it arises through conjunction and disjunction, it arises through a change of state, it arises through death and rebirth, it arises through the dissolution and evolution [of the world], it arises in the prior period, it arises at the time of death, it arises in the intermediate period, and it arises at the time of rebirth-linking.
What is the unarisen? How many are unarisen? For what purpose is the investigation of the unarisen?
That which is future and that which is unconditioned are unarisen;
this constitutes a portion of all [phenomena].
It is for the purpose of abandoning the adherence to a permanent self.
Furthermore, that which has not arisen is the opposite of that which has arisen.
What is the grasper? How many are the graspers? For what purpose is the examination of the grasper?
The material sense faculties, as well as the mind and mental factors, should be regarded as the grasper.
[They comprise] three aggregates, a portion of the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations, twelve elements, six bases, and a portion of the element and base of phenomena.
The self is the enjoyer, for the purpose of generating attachment.

Furthermore, there are apprehenders that do not reach their object, those that reach it, those that apprehend individual objects according to their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) in the present, and those that apprehend all objects at all times according to both their own and general characteristics (svasāmānyalakṣaṇa).

These various types of apprehenders are established based on the arising of consciousness through a causal complex (sāmagrī); moreover, the discourse regarding an "apprehender" should be understood as merely conventional (prajñaptika).
How is the object of apprehension (grāhya) defined? How many are the objects of apprehension? For what purpose is the investigation of the object of apprehension?
Whatever is an apprehending subject (grāhaka) is also an object of apprehension; however, there may be an object of apprehension that is not an apprehending subject.
The object is precisely the domain of the grasper;
all [objects of grasping] are for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to the self-nature of objects.
What is the outward-directed? How many are outward-directed? For what purpose is the examination of the outward-directed?

That which is associated with the desire realm is outward-directed, excluding the mental states and mental factors associated with the Buddha’s teaching that are comprised of those arisen from hearing, those arisen from reflection, and those sustained by the Dharma in accordance with it. Furthermore, four elements, two bases, and a portion of the others are outward-directed.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that has not yet transcended passion.
What is the inward-directed [mind]? What are the inward-directed [faculties]? For what purpose is the examination of the inward-directed?
The inward-directed is the opposite of the outward-directed.
Excluding four elements and two bases, it consists of a portion of the others;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is free from passion.
(Abhidh-s 21) What is the defiled? How many are defiled? For what purpose is the investigation of the defiled?

That which is unwholesome (*akuśala*) and that which is obstructed-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) is defiled. Furthermore, the obstructed-unspecified consists of the universal mental afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with the mind, as well as those bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
A portion of the aggregates, ten of the elements, and four of the sense-bases;
for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self associated with the afflictions.

What is the undefiled? How many are undefiled? For what purpose is the investigation of the undefiled? That which is wholesome or unobscured-neutral is undefiled. There are eight elements (dhātu), eight bases (āyatana), and a portion of the aggregates (skandha) as well as a portion of the remaining elements and bases.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is dissociated from the afflictions.
What is the past? How many things are past? For what purpose is the investigation of the past?

It is [defined] by way of its characteristic of having arisen and ceased; by way of having passed beyond cause, fruit, and utility; by way of having transcended the activity of affliction and purification; by way of the destruction of the grasping of causes; by way of the existence and non-existence of the specific characteristics of the fruit; and by way of being the object-sign for recollection and conceptualization.

The past should be viewed as a single portion of all [dharmas], both from the perspective of the signs of affliction through dependence and from the perspective of the signs of purification through equanimity;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that acts as a driver.
What is the future? How many things are future? For what purpose is the examination of the future?

[It is examined] because, although the cause exists, it has not yet arisen; because its own characteristic has not been acquired; because the cause and fruit have not yet functioned; because the states of affliction and purification have not yet manifested; because the intrinsic nature of the cause does not yet exist; and because there are the signs of both the affliction of delighting [in existence] and the purification of delighting [in liberation].
The future should also be viewed in this way;
it is a portion of all [the aggregates].
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that acts as an initiator.
How is the present defined? How many things are present? For what purpose is the investigation of the present undertaken?

The present should be understood from the following perspectives: by way of its characteristic of having arisen but not yet ceased; by way of the utilization or non-utilization of cause and fruit; by way of the manifestation of affliction or purification; by way of being the sign of past and future existence; and by way of the manifestation of functional activity.
It is a single portion of all [the aggregates],
intended solely for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that causes [samsaric] activity.

Furthermore, the subject matter of discourse (*kathāvastu*) pertains to the past, future, and present, but not to *nirvāṇa*; this is because *nirvāṇa* is to be personally realized within oneself and is thus inexpressible, and because it does not serve as a basis for the exclusion of what has been, what is to be, or what is currently occurring.
What is the wholesome? How many are wholesome? For what purpose is the investigation of the wholesome?
[It is investigated] by way of intrinsic nature, by way of association, by way of consequence, by way of origination, by way of ultimate reality, and by way of acquisition through birth.
The wholesome should be understood in terms of its application, its precedence, its favoring, its grasping, its counteractive nature, its pacification, and its natural outflow;
it constitutes a portion of the [five] aggregates, ten elements, and four bases.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self endowed with dharmas.
What is wholesome by its own nature? It consists of the eleven mental factors, beginning with faith.
What is wholesome by way of association? It refers to those factors associated with it.
What is the wholesome by way of consequence? It is the very latencies of those [wholesome states].
What is the wholesome by way of origination?
It is bodily action and vocal action originated by that [wholesome mind].
What is wholesome from the perspective of ultimate reality?
Suchness.
What is the wholesome [state] acquired by birth (*upapattilābhataḥ*)?
It is the manifestation of a maturation (*vipāka*) of such a nature, resulting from previous practice of these very same wholesome factors,
such that a natural inclination toward them arises even without deliberate reflection (*apratisaṃkhyāya*).
What is the wholesome by way of application?
It is the cultivation of the wholesome based upon attending upon virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, proper mental attention, and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is merit arising from a lotus?

It is the act of worship performed toward a Tathāgata—whether by placing him before one, or toward a shrine, or toward a book, or toward a painting—or toward the Dharma—by placing the Dharma before one, or performing worship toward a book that is the locus of the Dharma.
What is the wholesome by way of favor? It is that which belongs to one who favors sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
What is the wholesome by way of acquisition?

It is the acquisition of rebirth in heaven, or the acquisition of birth in a wealthy family, or the acquisition of conditions conducive to purification, through the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving or that consisting in ethical discipline. What is the wholesome by way of the antidote?

What is the wholesome [state] by way of pacification? It is that which is the counteragent of revulsion, the counteragent of support, the counteragent of distancing, the counteragent of suppression, the counteragent of dissociation, the counteragent of the obscuration of afflictions, and the counteragent of the obscuration of the knowable;
it is the abandonment of attachment through its exhaustion, the abandonment of hatred through its exhaustion, and the abandonment of delusion through its exhaustion.
The abandonment of all afflictions, the cessation of perception and feeling, the realm of nirvana with remainder, the realm of nirvana without remainder, and non-abiding nirvana.
What is the wholesome by way of outflow?

It refers to the distinguished qualities—such as the superknowledges (abhijñā) and so forth, whether mundane or supramundane, common or uncommon—which belong to one who has attained tranquility (upaśama) through the sovereign influence of that [wholesome state].
What is the unwholesome? How many are the unwholesome? For what purpose is the investigation of the unwholesome?

[It is investigated] by way of intrinsic nature, by way of connection, by way of consequence, by way of origination, by way of ultimate reality, by way of acquisition at birth, by way of application, by way of veneration, by way of injury, and by way of appropriation. (Abhidh-s 23)
The unwholesome should be viewed both as an adverse factor and as an obstacle;
it constitutes a portion of the aggregates, ten elements, and four bases.
It is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is joined with unrighteousness.

What is unwholesome by its very nature? It is any affliction or secondary affliction other than those associated with the mind and those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness—excluding the latter—which gives rise to misconduct.
What is unwholesome by way of association? It refers to those phenomena associated with those very same afflictions and secondary afflictions.
What is unwholesome by way of its consequence?
It is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) of those very [unwholesome states].
What is unwholesome by way of origination? It is bodily and vocal action that has been originated [by such a mind].
What is unwholesome in the ultimate sense?
All of saṃsāra.
What is unwholesome by way of acquisition at birth?
Just as, through the habitual practice of unwholesome states, a corresponding ripening result arises by which a taste for what is unwholesome alone becomes established.

What is unwholesome by way of application? It is as follows: having come upon association with bad persons, hearing the non-dharmic teaching, and improper mental attention, one engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.

What is unwholesome by way of motivation? It is when, for instance, having placed one’s reliance upon or honored some particular class of gods, one establishes a shrine preceded by violence or preceded by wrong views, or performs acts of worship there, whereby a great multitude of people becomes joined with demerit.
What is unwholesome by way of harm? It is when one engages in wrong conduct toward sentient beings through body, speech, or mind.
What is unwholesome by way of acquisition?

It is when, having practiced misconduct with the body, or having practiced misconduct with speech and mind, one acquires an undesirable fruit—whether it be in an unfortunate rebirth or a fortunate rebirth—which is either projective or completing.
What is unwholesome by way of opposition?
Those phenomena which are the counteragents and their opposites.
What is unwholesome regarding the path? It refers to those factors that obstruct the wholesome.
What is the indeterminate? How many are indeterminate? For what purpose is the investigation of the indeterminate?

[It is investigated] by way of intrinsic nature, by way of connection, by way of consequence, by way of origination, by way of ultimate reality, by way of acquisition through birth, by way of application, by way of veneration, by way of favor, by way of enjoyment, by way of appropriation, and by way of antidote.
Furthermore, it should be asked whether [the unconditioned] is indeterminate in terms of its pacification (*upaśama*), its outflow (*niṣyanda*), or both.
Eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*), as well as a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases, constitute this category.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is dissociated from both dharma and adharma.
What is that which is indeterminate by its very nature?

It consists of the eight material elements and bases, the mental faculty together with its associated states, the life-faculty, the homogeneous character of a group, and the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.
What is the indeterminate by way of association?
It refers to the mental states and mental factors associated with those very sets of names, phrases, and syllables in one whose mind is neither defiled nor serene.
What is neutral by way of consequence?
It is the latencies of verbal expression for those very [actions].
What is neutral by way of origination?
It is the action of body and speech that is originated by the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) embraced by that [volition].
What is indeterminate from the perspective of ultimate truth?
It is space and cessation not through deliberation.
What is the indeterminate by way of acquisition at birth?
It is the maturation (vipāka) of unwholesome factors and wholesome-with-outflows factors.
What is the indeterminate by way of application? It is the conduct pertaining to postures and the conduct pertaining to crafts, which arise from a mind that is neither afflicted nor unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate by way of dedication (*puraskārato ’vyākṛtam*)?

It is as follows: having dedicated oneself to reliance upon one or another class of gods, one establishes a shrine (*caitya*) or performs an act of worship that is free from violence and wrong views, wherein the great mass of people does not [perceive] merit.
It does not produce demerit.
What is the indeterminate [action] by way of favor?
It is, for example, when one gives a gift to slaves, laborers, or servants, or to one's wife and children, with a mind that is neither defiled nor serene.
What is neutral by way of enjoyment?
It is when one enjoys possessions with a mind that is neither analytical nor afflicted.
What is the indeterminate by way of appropriation?
It is when, due to the habitual practice of a craft, one acquires in the future a corresponding physical basis such that one very easily reaches the culmination of training in those crafts.
What is the indeterminate by way of counteragent?
Just as one partakes of medicine after having reflected upon it.
What is the indeterminate by way of tranquility?
It is the affliction belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, based on its being concealed by calm abiding (*śamatha*).
What is the indeterminate nature by way of outflow? It is that which arises simultaneously with the mind of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, by way of illustration, it should be understood that there is also the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
What, then, is that?
