That which the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas who have attained the supreme perfection manifest for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—yet for them there is no such actual completion therein.
How is it associated with the desire realm? How many are associated with the desire realm? For what purpose is the investigation of those associated with the desire realm?
For one who is not free from passion, the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are to be understood as bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This includes the four elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the other aggregates, elements, and bases.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is not free from passion for the desire realm.
What are the factors associated with the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)? For what purpose is the investigation of those associated with the realm of form?

Those that are wholesome or neutral for one who is free from desire for the realm of desire but not yet free from desire for the realm of form should be understood as associated with the realm of form.
Excluding four elements and two bases, it consists of a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is free from passion for the realm of desire.
What is associated with the formless realm? How many [factors] are associated with the formless realm? For what purpose is the investigation of those associated with the formless realm?
That which is wholesome or neutral for one who is free from passion for the form realm but not yet free from passion for the formless realm should be understood as associated with the formless realm.
It consists of a portion of four aggregates and two bases.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is free from passion for form.

Furthermore, detachment (*vairāgya*) should be understood as partial detachment, complete detachment, detachment through penetration, detachment through impairment, and detachment through eradication.
Moreover, there are indeed ten types of detachment:
natural detachment, detachment through impairment, detachment through support, detachment through excellence, and detachment through delusion.
Detachment through counteraction, detachment through full comprehension, detachment through abandonment, detachment with something superior, and unsurpassed detachment.
What is natural detachment? It is the state of aversion toward painful feeling and toward those phenomena that are conducive to suffering.
What is detachment through suppression?
It is the state of aversion that arises when the burning sensation of one engaged in sexual intercourse has subsided.
What is detachment through support? It is the sense of aversion toward even delicious food in one who has eaten well.
What is detachment through superiority? It is the state of aversion toward an inferior state by one who has attained a higher station.
What is delusive detachment? It is the aversion toward nirvāṇa found among the foolish.
What is detachment through the counteragent?
It is the abandonment of the afflictions by means of either the mundane or the supramundane path.
What is detachment through full comprehension?
It is the state of aversion toward the three realms belonging to one who has attained the path of vision.
What is detachment through abandonment? It is the state of aversion toward the afflictions as one abandons them stage by stage.
What is inferior detachment?
It is the detachment belonging to worldly beings, as well as to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is unsurpassed detachment?
It is the detachment of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, based upon their commitment to the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.

What is the state of training (śaikṣa)? How many are states of training? For what purpose is the investigation of the state of training? The wholesome [states] of one engaged in liberation are to be regarded as the state of training.
It constitutes a portion of the aggregates, ten of the elements, and four of the sense-bases (āyatana).
For the purpose of causing the abandonment of the attachment to a self that is engaged in liberation.

What is the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)? How many things belong to one beyond training? For what purpose is the investigation of those beyond training? The wholesome [states] of one who has reached the culmination of training are to be regarded as belonging to one beyond training. This consists of a portion of the aggregates (skandhas), ten elements (dhātus), and four bases (āyatanas).
This is for the purpose of abandoning the deep-seated attachment to a self that has been experienced.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner? How many are neither-learner-nor-non-learners? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

The wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [dharmas] of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana); the afflicted and neutral [dharmas] of a learner (śaikṣa); the neutral [dharmas] and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of a non-learner (aśaikṣa)—these should be regarded as neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Eight elements (dhātu), eight bases (āyatana), and the remainder of the other [factors] are [neither-learner-nor-non-learner].
It is a portion of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases,
for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a non-liberated self.
What is to be abandoned by seeing? How many are to be abandoned by seeing? For what purpose is the investigation of what is to be abandoned by seeing?

The imagined afflicted view, doubt, the basis for views, those afflictions and secondary afflictions that are mistaken regarding views, all bodily and vocal karma originated by views, and all aggregates, elements, and sense-fields pertaining to the miserable destinies—all this should be understood as what is to be abandoned by seeing.
It is a single portion of all [the truths],
for the purpose of abandoning the self-clinging of those who possess the vision [of the truths].
What is to be abandoned by cultivation? How many are to be abandoned by cultivation? For what purpose is the investigation of what is to be abandoned by cultivation?
For one who has attained the path of seeing, it consists of all contaminated phenomena that exist subsequent to that, which are the opposite of those to be abandoned by seeing;
it is a portion of all [phenomena].
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is perfected through cultivation.
What is not to be abandoned? How many are not to be abandoned? For what purpose is the investigation of that which is not to be abandoned?
That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is to be regarded as not to be abandoned, with the exception of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
It constitutes a portion of the aggregates, ten of the elements, and four of the sense-bases.
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to the notion of a self that has been established.
What is dependently originated? How many things are dependently originated? For what purpose is the investigation of the dependently originated?

[It is examined] by way of its characteristics, by way of the analysis of its members, by way of the summary of its members, by way of the determination of the conditionality of its members, by way of the determination of the functions of its members, by way of the inclusion of its members within the defilements, by way of its meaning, by way of its profundity, by way of its divisions, and by way of its forward and reverse order.
These too should be seen as dependently originated,
with the exception of a portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is causeless or has discordant causes.
How [is it] by way of its characteristics?
By virtue of arising from conditions that are effortless, by virtue of arising from conditions that are impermanent, and by virtue of arising from conditions that are efficacious.
How is it analyzed by way of its constituent parts?
There are twelve parts;

dependent origination consists of twelve parts: ignorance, formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death.
How [is it] even by way of the summary of the members?
There are the projecting member, the projected member, the actualizing member, and the actualized member.
What is the projecting limb?
It is ignorance, formative forces, and consciousness.
What is the projected limb?
It is name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
What is the limb of actualization?
It is craving, grasping, and becoming. What is the limb of birth?
Birth, as well as old age and death.
How is the establishment of the factors as conditions to be understood?

It should be understood that the establishment of the factors as conditions occurs through habituation (*vāsanā*), through impelling (*āvedha*), through mental attention (*manasikāra*), and through coexistence (*sahabhāva*), according to their respective applications.
How is it established by way of the functions of its factors?
What is the function of ignorance?
It deludes sentient beings regarding existence and serves as a condition.
It occurs with respect to the formative forces (saṃskāra).
What is the function of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?
They differentiate sentient beings within the realms of existence and serve as conditions for the latencies of consciousness (*vijñāna-vāsanā*).
What is the function of consciousness?
It sustains the bondage of karma for sentient beings and serves as the condition for name-and-form.
And what is the function of name-and-form?
It causes sentient beings to grasp a personal existence and serves as the condition for the six sense bases.
What is the function of the six sense bases?
It causes sentient beings to grasp the fulfillment of their own existence and serves as the condition for contact.
What is the function of contact?
It causes sentient beings to engage in the enjoyment of sense objects and serves as the condition for sensation.
What is the function of sensation?
It causes sentient beings to engage in the experience of birth and serves as the condition for craving.
What is the function of craving?
It draws sentient beings toward rebirth and serves as the condition for grasping.
What is the function of clinging (*upādāna*)?
It serves to take up renewed existence (*punarbhava*), and it makes the consciousness of sentient beings possessed of clinging (*sopādāna*), while also acting as the condition for becoming (*bhava*).
What is the function of becoming (*bhava*)?
It brings sentient beings face-to-face with renewed existence and serves as the condition for birth (*jāti*).
What is the function of birth?
It brings sentient beings into existence through the successive stages of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, and it serves as the condition for aging and death.
What is the function of aging and death?
It repeatedly yokes sentient beings to the transformation of their youth and the transformation of their life.
How is there a summary by way of the afflictions of the members?
That which is ignorance, that which is craving, and that which is grasping—this is the summary of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Those which are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), that which is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and that which is becoming (*bhava*)—this is the summary of the affliction of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*).
The remaining [factors] are included within the defilement of birth.
In what sense?
The meaning of dependent origination is the meaning of being without an agent;
it is the meaning of having causes, the meaning of being devoid of a sentient being, the meaning of being dependent on others, and the meaning of being without a creator.

The meaning of dependent origination consists of the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of momentariness, the meaning of the non-interruption of the continuity of cause and fruit, the meaning of corresponding causes and fruits, the meaning of diverse causes and fruits, and the meaning of specific causes and fruits.
How is its profundity to be understood?

Profundity is to be seen in terms of the profundity of the cause, the profundity of the characteristic, the profundity of the portion of arising, the profundity of duration, and the profundity of the mode of operation.
Furthermore, dependent origination is indeed momentary, yet it is also perceived in terms of stability;
dependent origination has inactive conditions, yet it is also perceived as having efficacious conditions;
dependent origination is devoid of a sentient being, yet it is also perceived in terms of a self.
It is not arisen from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor is it produced without a cause by itself or by another;
for this reason also, it is profound.
How is it [classified] by way of differentiation?

By way of the differentiation of the arising of consciousness; by way of the differentiation of death and rebirth; by way of the differentiation of the arising of external crops; and by way of the differentiation of the dissolution and evolution [of the world].

The classification [of giving] is to be understood through the distinction of support by means of food, the distinction of the division between desirable and undesirable destinies, the distinction of purification, and the distinction of power.
How is it [taught] in direct and reverse order?

The exposition of dependent origination in direct and reverse order should be understood both from the perspective of the direct and reverse order of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), and also from the perspective of the direct and reverse order of purification (*vyavadāna*).
(Now, in the first section on the three phenomena within the Fundamental Subjects, the third part:
How is a condition? How many conditions are there? For what purpose is the investigation of conditions?
A condition should be understood from the perspective of cause, immediate succession, object, and predominance.
All [phenomena] are conditions;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to phenomena that have the self as their cause.
What is the causal condition?
It is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the latencies of the wholesome.

Furthermore, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) should be understood by way of its intrinsic nature, its differentiation, its companions, its correct engagement, its obstacles, and its appropriation.
How is it by way of intrinsic nature?
It is the cause by way of the intrinsic nature of the cause.
How [is it] by way of classification?
It is the cause of origination, such as the collection of conditions for visual consciousness.
The cause of maintenance is, for example, food for beings who have come into existence and those seeking birth.
The cause of support is, for example, the earth for sentient beings.
An illuminating cause is, for example, a lamp for visible forms.
The cause of transformation is, for example, fire in relation to fuel.
The cause of separation is, for example, a sickle in relation to that which is to be cut.
The cause of transformation is, for example, craftsmanship and the like with respect to gold and other such materials.
The cause of conviction is, for example, smoke [as proof] of fire.
The cause of persuasion is, for example, the proposition, the reason, and the example [as proofs] of that which is to be established.
The cause of attainment is, for example, the path to nirvana.
The causes of conventional usage are as follows: namely, name, conceptualization, and view.
The causal condition of dependence (*apekṣākāraṇa*) is that in relation to which a desire for something arises;
for example, in relation to hunger, there is a desire for food.
The projecting cause is a remote condition;
for example, ignorance [is the projecting cause] of aging and death.
The cause of actualization is the proximate condition;
for example, ignorance is [the cause] of the formative forces.
The cause of appropriation is another condition; for example, the field, water, and manure are the conditions for the arising of a crop.
A productive cause is a condition by way of conformity; for example, the proper service of a king is the condition for pleasing the king.
The cause of specific restriction is the diversity of conditions;
for example, the conditions for the five destinies are the five destinies themselves.
The auxiliary cause is the collection of conditions;
for example, in the case of consciousness, it consists of an unimpaired sense faculty, an object that has come into range, and the corresponding attention that has arisen.
An obstructive cause is an impediment;
for example, lightning striking a crop.
The cause of non-obstruction is the absence of an obstacle;
that is to say, the non-existence of that very obstacle.
How is it by way of association?
Those dharmas that arise through coexistence and not through the deficiency of even one [of them],
such as the primary elements (bhūta) and the derivative matter (bhautika).
How is it by way of correct engagement?
Those phenomena which, through their coexistence, engage with the object of focus, and not when even one of them is lacking.
Namely, the mind and mental factors.
How is it [understood] from the perspective of nourishment?
It is the subsequent occurrence of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena—previously cultivated—which becomes increasingly more nourished and most highly nourished in the future limit.
How is it by way of being an obstacle?
It is the strengthening and solidification of the continuity of any one of the afflictions through the cultivation of any one of them,
for the purpose of distancing oneself from the continuum of nirvāṇa.
How [are they] by way of appropriation? Unwholesome factors and wholesome-with-outflows factors [are so called] because they appropriate a personal existence.

How is the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) to be understood? It should be understood both from the perspective of immediate succession and from the perspective of uninterrupted immediate succession, as well as from the perspective of the arising of similar and dissimilar minds and mental factors (citta-caitta).

How is it by way of the object? It is by way of having a delimited object as its object, by way of having an undelimited object as its object, by way of having an object that is not characterized by variety [or,

having an object that is characterized by variety], by way of having a basis in reality as the training's object, by way of having an object that lacks a basis in reality, by way of having a real entity as its object, and by way of having a conceptual construction as its object.

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) should be understood from the perspective of being an inverted object, as well as a non-inverted object; and from the perspective of being an obstructed object, as well as an unobstructed object.

How is it by way of predominance? It is by way of the predominance of the foundation, by way of the predominance of the impulse, by way of the predominance of coexistence, by way of the predominance of the object,
by way of the predominance of production, by way of the predominance of location, by way of the predominance of the enjoyment of the fruit, and by way of mundane purity.
The dominant condition should be understood both from the perspective of its predominance and from the perspective of supramundane purity.

How are [the sense bases] "functioning" (sabhāga) and "non-functioning" (tatsabhāga)? How many are functioning and non-functioning? For what purpose is the investigation of the functioning and non-functioning performed?

The functioning and non-functioning should be understood as follows: [they are so called] because of the arising of a continuity of sense faculties and objects that are not devoid of consciousness and which resemble them, and also because of the arising of a continuity that resembles itself even when devoid of consciousness.

They constitute a portion of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), namely the five material elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana). This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is either conjoined with or disjoined from consciousness.
How is it appropriated? How many are appropriated? For what purpose is the investigation of the appropriated?
It should be understood that [matter] is appropriated by virtue of being the basis for the arising of sensation.
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), namely the five material elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of four others;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that exercises mastery over the body.
What is a faculty (*indriya*), how many faculties are there, and for what purpose is the investigation of the faculties?

[They are investigated] by way of their sovereignty over the apprehension of objects, their sovereignty over the continuity of the wholesome, their sovereignty over abiding in a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*),
their sovereignty over the enjoyment of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma, their sovereignty over mundane detachment, and their sovereignty over supramundane detachment.
The faculty should also be viewed as such:

it consists of the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of consciousness, a portion of the aggregates of form and mental formations, the twelve elements, the six sense bases, and a portion of the element and base of phenomena.
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to the notion of self-sovereignty.
What is the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*)? How many are the instances of suffering as suffering? For what purpose is the investigation of suffering as suffering undertaken?

Suffering as suffering should be understood both from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of painful feeling itself and from the specific characteristic of those phenomena that are to be experienced as painful.
It constitutes a portion of all [phenomena].
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is suffering.
What is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), how many are the sufferings of change, and for what purpose is the investigation of the suffering of change?

The suffering of change consists of: the specific characteristic of the transformation of pleasant feeling; the specific characteristic of the transformation of those phenomena to be experienced as pleasant; and the transformation of the mind characterized by attachment toward them.
It comprises a portion of all [phenomena].
For the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that is happy.

What is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? How many types of the suffering of conditioned formations are there? For what purpose is the investigation of the suffering of conditioned formations undertaken? The suffering of conditioned formations is to be seen as follows: from the perspective of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; from the perspective of the characteristic of its own factors that are to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant; from the perspective of being encompassed by the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) of both [pain and pleasure]; and from the perspective of being insecure due to the lack of liberation from the two [extremes] and the continuous connection with impermanence.
Excluding a portion of three aggregates, three elements, and two bases, all [remaining phenomena] are included;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the deep-seated attachment to a self that is neither painful nor pleasant.
How is there maturation? How many things have maturation? For what purpose is the investigation of that which has maturation?
That which is unwholesome and that which is wholesome but associated with outflows should be seen as having maturation.
This includes a portion of the aggregates, ten of the elements, and four of the sense-bases.
It is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that casts off the aggregates and reassembles them.
Furthermore, the maturation (vipāka) should be understood as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) together with its associated mental factors;
that which is other than this is born of maturation (vipākaja).
What is nutriment? How many nutriments are there? For what purpose is the investigation of nutriment?
Nutriment should be understood from four perspectives: by way of transformation (*pāriṇāmika*), by way of object (*vaiṣayika*), by way of intention (*āśayika*), and by way of grasping (*upādānika*).
It consists of a portion of three aggregates, eleven elements, and five bases;
it is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self that subsists through nutriment.

Furthermore, nutriment should be understood as that which subsists upon an impure basis, that which subsists upon both pure and impure bases, that which subsists upon a pure basis, and that which demonstrates stability.
How is there something "surpassable" (*sottara*)?
How many things are surpassable? For what purpose is the investigation of the surpassable?
That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and a portion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should be regarded as surpassable.
Excluding one portion of the sphere and base of the dharma-element, all [others] are included;
this is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to a self-substance that is devoid of reality.
How is it unsurpassed? How many are unsurpassed? For what purpose is the investigation of the unsurpassed?
It should be understood as unsurpassed from the perspective of a portion of the unconditioned;
it is a portion of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
This is for the purpose of abandoning the attachment to the self as a supreme substance;
by this method, the system of classification is immeasurable.
Furthermore, in brief, the classification of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields is threefold:
the classification of the imagined characteristic, the classification of the discriminated characteristic, and the classification of the characteristic of the true nature of phenomena.
In that regard, what is the differentiation of the imagined characteristic?
It is that which is imagined among the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields as a self, or as a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, a human, or a youth.
What is the differentiation of the characteristics of conceptual construction?
It consists of those very aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

What is the differentiation of the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? It is the absence of a self within those very aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; it is the absence of a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, a human, or a man; it is the existence of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Furthermore, there are four kinds of distinctions:
the distinction of characteristics, the distinction of types, the distinction of non-exhaustion, and the distinction of continuity.
What is the differentiation by characteristics?
It is the differentiation of the specific characteristics of each of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
The classification of types:

these very aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are categorized as having substantial existence, having conceptual existence, having conventional existence, or having ultimate existence; likewise, they are classified as being with form or formless, visible or invisible, and so forth, as previously explained.
What is the differentiation of the basis?
There are as many aggregates, elements, and sense-fields as there are bases for sentient beings.
What is the differentiation of the continuum? It is the moment-to-moment occurrence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What does one who is skilled in the distinctions of characteristics thoroughly understand?
One thoroughly understands the adherence to a self.
What does one who is skilled in the distinctions of types thoroughly understand?
One thoroughly understands the notion of a composite whole.
Being skilled in the differentiation of the basis, what does one fully understand?
One fully understands the notion that there is neither the acquisition of what was not done nor the loss of what was done.
One who is skilled in the differentiation of the continuity [of existence] thoroughly understands what?
One thoroughly understands the notion of stability.
Furthermore, there is a sixfold classification of these very aggregates, elements, and sense-bases:

the classification of the outward-turned, the classification of the inward-turned, the classification of long duration, the classification of limited duration, the classification of that specific time, and the classification of demonstration.
What is the classification of the outward-turned?
For the most part, it consists of the various subdivisions of the desire realm.
What is the internal classification?
It consists of all the stages of meditative concentration (samādhi).
What is the distinction regarding long duration?
It is that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

What is the classification by delimited time? It refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases of those in training (*śaikṣa*), excluding their final moment, as well as those of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) other than that [final moment].
What is the classification by time?
It consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases at the final moment of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is the differentiation by way of manifestation?
It consists of the manifest aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the Buddhas who have attained the perfections and of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
(Now, in the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, within the section on the fundamental subjects, the second chapter is the "Compendium").
What is compendium?
Compendium should be understood as being of eleven kinds.

The inclusion by way of characteristics, the inclusion by way of elements, the inclusion by way of genus, the inclusion by way of state, the inclusion by way of companions, the inclusion by way of location, the inclusion by way of time, the inclusion by way of a single part, the inclusion by way of the whole, the inclusion by way of mutual relation, and the inclusion by way of ultimate reality.
What is the summary by way of characteristics? It is the inclusion of each of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases by means of its own specific characteristic.
What is the inclusion of the elements?
It is the inclusion of each respective element by means of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as the seed for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is inclusion by way of genus?
It is the mutual inclusion of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, even though they possess distinct characteristics, within the categories of aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
What is the summary by way of states?
It is the summary by way of their own characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields that exist in states of pleasure,
as well as those in states of suffering and those in states that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Based on the state.
What is the inclusion by way of companions?
The aggregate of form is included as distinct from the other aggregates by virtue of its companions;
likewise for the other aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is inclusion by way of location?

It is the inclusion, by means of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) that depend on the eastern direction.
In the same way, this should be understood for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the other directions as well.
What is the summary by way of time?
It is the summary of the past aggregates, elements, and sense-bases by means of their own specific characteristics;
and likewise for the future and present aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is inclusion by way of a single part?

It should be understood that inclusion by way of a single part is the inclusion of any one among those phenomena, however many they may be, that are included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is the complete inclusion?

It should be understood that the complete inclusion consists of the inclusion, without exception, of as many phenomena as there are that are included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
What is mutual inclusion? In the inclusion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), how many elements (*dhātu*) and how many bases (*āyatana*) are there?
A portion of ten [elements and bases].
In the inclusion of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), how many elements and how many bases are there?
A single part;
as is the aggregate of sensation, so too are the aggregates of perception and mental formations.
In the inclusion of the aggregate of consciousness, how many elements (dhātu) and how many bases (āyatana) are there?
Seven elements and one base.
In the inclusion of the eye-element, how many aggregates and how many bases are there?
A portion of the aggregate of form; one base.
The eye-element, and likewise the ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible-object elements.
In the inclusion of the mind-element (manodhātu), how many aggregates (skandha) and how many bases (āyatana) are there?
One aggregate and one base.
In the inclusion within the dharma-sphere (dharmadhātu), how many aggregates (skandhas) and how many bases (āyatanas) are there?
There are three aggregates, a portion of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), and one base.

Regarding the inclusion within the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), how many aggregates (*skandha*) and how many bases (*āyatana*) are there? They consist of a portion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*). As with the visual consciousness element, so it is with the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements (*śrotra-ghrāṇa-jihvā-kāya-manovijñānadhātavaḥ*).
In the inclusion of the eye-base (cakṣurāyatana), how many aggregates (skandha) and how many elements (dhātu) are there?
It is one part of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and one element.
Just as it is with the eye-base, so it is with the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
In the inclusion of the mind-base (manāyatana), how many aggregates (skandha) and how many elements (dhātu) are there?
One aggregate and seven elements. In the inclusion of the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana), how many aggregates and how many elements are there?
A portion of three aggregates and one element.

In the same way, other phenomena (dharmas) are indicated by means of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana), while others are not indicated by the aggregates, elements, and bases.

These have been previously demonstrated as having substantiality (dravyavat), being designations (prajñaptimat), being conventional (saṃvṛtimat), being ultimate (paramārthavat), being knowable (jñeya), being cognizable (vijñeya), being to be directly realized (abhijñeya), being material (rūpin), being immaterial (arūpin), being visible (sanidarśana), being invisible (anidarśana), and so forth.
Their mutual inclusion by means of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases should be understood according to their respective applications.

What is the summary of the ultimate truth? One who is skilled in the summary of the suchness of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases obtains what benefit? One obtains the benefit of the condensation [of the mind] upon the object of focus.
To the extent that there is a concentration of the mind upon objects of focus, to that same extent there is an increase in the roots of virtue.
(Now, in the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, within the section on the Fundamental Bases, this is the third chapter: Concordance.
What is concordance?
Briefly stated, concordance is of six kinds.

There is association through non-separation, association through commingling, association through coexistence, association through co-occurrence, association through the performance of a task, and association through concordant realization.
What is association through non-separation?
It is the mutual non-separation of all spatially extended parts of matter that are comprised within atoms.
What is the conjunction of mingling?
It is the mutual mingling of all spatially situated portions of form from the second atom upward.
What is conjunction through coexistence? It is the coexistence of constituent parts belonging to the same location within a continuous series of forms.
What is concomitance by coexistence (*sahabhāva-saṃprayoga*)?
It is the simultaneous occurrence, arising, abiding, and cessation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases within a single body.
What is concomitance by the performance of a function (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-saṃprayoga*)?
In the performance of a single task, there is mutual association;
for example, when two monks perform an action, one monk’s performance of that action constitutes this association with the other.

What is the association of common engagement (*saṃpratipatti-saṃprayoga*)? It is the mutual common engagement of the mind and mental factors upon a single object. Furthermore, this association of common engagement has multiple meanings.

Just as association occurs through the nature of another (*parabhāva*) and not through its own nature (*svabhāva*), so too association occurs between two things that are non-contradictory and not between two things that are contradictory;

it occurs between those of similar time and not between those of dissimilar time; and it occurs between those belonging to the same realm (*dhātu*) and stage (*bhūmi*) and not between those belonging to different realms.
In the two stages.
Universal association refers, for example, to feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, and consciousness.
Furthermore, the afflicted universal association consists of the four afflictions in relation to the mind.
Occasional association is, for example, that of the wholesome factors such as faith and so forth, or of the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment and so forth, with the mind.
The situational association refers to the association of pleasant feeling together with its associated mental factors;
likewise for painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
In a state with mind, the association is uninterrupted;
for one who has been interrupted by an attainment without mind, the association is severed.
Outward-directed conjunction refers primarily to the mind and mental factors associated with the realm of desire.
Internal application is, for the most part, the association of the mind and mental factors belonging to the stages of meditative concentration.
The appropriate association belongs to the minds and mental factors of ordinary persons, and to some among those in training and those beyond training.
Improper application refers to the initial and subsequent supramundane minds and mental factors, as well as those acquired subsequent to the supramundane state.
What benefit does one who is skilled in association obtain?
One knows the association within the mind alone of those factors that are defiling—such as feeling—and those that are purifying.
Knowing this, one experiences, perceives, wills, and remembers; one becomes defiled or purified; one wills, abandons attachment, and enters into selflessness.
(Abhidh-s 35) (Now, in the Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra, within the section on the Fundamental Subjects, this is the fourth chapter: the Analysis of Possession.
What is possession (*samanvāgama*)?
In terms of its characteristics, it is as previously described.
Furthermore, its classification is threefold:
possession of seeds, possession of mastery, and possession of manifest activity.

What is the possession of seeds? One born and arisen in the desire realm is possessed of the possession of seeds of the afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the desire realm, as well as those associated with the form and formless realms, and of the wholesome states acquired at birth.

One born and existing in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) should be said to be both possessed of and not possessed of the seeds of the afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa) associated with the desire realm;
and one should be said to be both possessed of and not possessed of the seeds of the afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the realm of form and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
[In the formless realm...]
He is endowed with the primary and secondary afflictions through the possession of their seeds, and also with the wholesome states acquired at birth.
One who has attained the antidote to the three realms is no longer possessed of the possession of the seeds of whichever specific type for which the antidote has arisen;
however, one is still possessed of the possession of the seeds of that for which the antidote has not yet arisen.

What is the possession of mastery? It is being endowed with the possession of mastery over those dharmas produced through application— whether mundane or supramundane, such as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*)— and over certain neutral (*avyākṛta*) states.
What is possession through manifest activity?

It is the possession of whichever phenomenon—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—is currently manifest among the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, by means of that very phenomenon’s possession through manifest activity.
One whose roots of virtue have been severed should be said to be both possessed of and not possessed of the possession of the seeds of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, the ultimate possession of afflictions should be understood as belonging to the icchantikas, who by nature do not attain parinirvāṇa;
because they lack the cause for liberation, they possess an ultimate non-possession of that cause.
One who is skilled in thorough comprehension attains what benefit? One becomes a knower of the increase and decrease of phenomena.

Thus, being a knower of the increase and decrease [of phenomena], one does not form a notion of exclusivity toward any worldly prosperity or adversity, precisely for the sake of abandoning attachment and aversion.
In the Abhidharmasamuccaya, the first compendium, titled the Compendium of Characteristics, is concluded.
(Abhidh-s 36) [Now, in the Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra, within the Viniścayasaṃuccaya, the first chapter on the Analysis of Truths.
What is the definitive determination?
The determination of truth, the determination of phenomena, the determination of attainment, and the determination through discussion.
What is the determination of the truths?
They are the four noble truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
That [birth] should be understood in terms of the birth of sentient beings and the basis of birth.
What is the birth of sentient beings?
It is birth among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans in Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, Jambudvīpa, Uttarakuru, and among the gods of the four [great kings].

Among the Rājikāyikas, the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratīs, the Paranirmitavaśavartīs, the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmās, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttaśubhas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, the Bṛhatphalas, the Asaṃjñisattvas, the Avṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, the Akaniṣṭhas, the Ākāśānantyāyatanas, the Vijñānānantyāyatanas, and the Ākiṃcanyāyatanas.
In the spheres of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the basis of birth?
It is the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
Upon the circle of wind (vāyumaṇḍala) is established the circle of water (apmaṇḍala).
Within the water-circle is the earth-circle;
within the earth-circle are Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, the four continents, the eight intermediate islands,
the inner ocean, the outer ocean, the four terraces of Sumeru, and the dwellings of the Cāturmahārājakāyika and Trāyastriṃśa deities.

Other locations include the mountain Cakravāḍa, celestial palaces in the sky belonging to the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as well as those of the gods of the form realm (rūpāvacara), the various abodes of the asuras, and the various abodes of the hell-beings—
namely, the hot hells, the cold hells, and the individual hells— as well as certain other abodes of animals and hungry ghosts.
As far as the suns, while revolving, illuminate the directions as Vairocanas, so in a thousandfold world-system there are a thousand moons,
a thousand suns, a thousand Sumerus, kings of mountains, a thousand of each of the four continents,
a thousand of the gods of the Four Great Kings, a thousand of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and a thousand of the Yāma gods.
A thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmā-worlds— this is called a small chiliocosm (sahasracūḍika lokadhātu).
A thousand of thousands of relic-pagodas is called the second, the intermediate-thousandfold world system.
A thousand middle *sāhasra* realms is called the third, the *trisāhasramahāsāhasra* world-system.
Thus, that *trisāhasramahāsāhasra* world-system is encircled by the circular range of the Great Cakravāḍa mountains;
and that *trisāhasramahāsāhasra* world-system includes its cycles of dissolution and evolution.

And so, O Lord, the god rains down drops of rain in the shape of wheels, incessantly and without interruption, from the sky. And likewise, in the eastern direction, there is an immeasurable world-system that is incessant and uninterrupted, which is either undergoing dissolution, or undergoing evolution, or currently dissolving, or remaining dissolved, or currently evolving, or remaining evolved.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in all ten directions.

Both the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the world of the vessel (*bhājanaloka*)—produced by karma and afflictions (*karmakleśa*) and dominated by karma and afflictions—are called the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
However, a completely pure world-realm (*pariśuddhalokadhātu*) is not comprised within the truth of suffering; it is neither produced by karma and afflictions nor dominated by karma and afflictions.

It is drawn forth solely by the power of a great vow, which has the roots of merit conducive to purification as its dominant condition; and its place of arising is inconceivable, known only by a Buddha and not within the range of meditation for those who practice dhyāna, much less for those who engage in discursive thought.
Furthermore, there are eight specific classifications of the characteristic of suffering:

"Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the pleasant is suffering; not obtaining what one desires is also suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering."
On what basis is birth suffering?
It is suffering on the basis of its nature as a state of confinement and because it serves as the foundation for other sufferings.
On what basis is aging suffering?
Because it undergoes the state of suffering through transformation over time.
On what basis is illness suffering?
It is on the basis of the suffering of transformation within the primary elements.
On what basis is death suffering?
It is on the basis of the suffering of the destruction of life.
On what basis is association with the unpleasant suffering?
On the basis of the suffering born of conjunction.
On what basis is separation from the beloved suffering?
It is on the basis of the nature of suffering born of separation.
Furthermore, regarding that which one desires but does not obtain, on what basis is it suffering?
It is suffering on the basis of the state of suffering born from the absence of the desired fruit.
Briefly stated, why are the five aggregates of clinging suffering?
Because they consist of the suffering of dysfunctions.
Thus, these eight, when subsumed, become six:

the suffering of confinement, the suffering of transformation, the suffering of association, the suffering of dissociation, the suffering of the non-attainment of desired fruits, and the suffering of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Thus, by way of expansion, the six become eight;
the six, when combined, become eight.
Regarding what was said concerning the three types of suffering (*duḥkhatā*),
within them the eight sufferings are subsumed.
In that regard, how are the eight subsumed within the three, or how are the three subsumed within the eight?

Because it includes the characteristics of the successive [stages], birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the unpleasant is suffering—this is the suffering of suffering within the continuum.
Separation from the pleasant is suffering, and not obtaining what one desires is also suffering; this is the suffering of change.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering; that is the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations.
Regarding what was stated as "two kinds of suffering":
that refers to suffering by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and suffering by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
What is suffering by way of conventional truth? What is suffering by way of ultimate truth?
Birth is suffering, and so on, up to: even not obtaining what one desires is suffering; this is suffering according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As it was said in brief: "The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*) are suffering"; this is suffering according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
What is the general characteristic of the truth of suffering?
It is the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of emptiness, and the characteristic of non-self.
What is the characteristic of impermanence?
In brief, it is of twelve kinds:

the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of destruction, the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of separation, the characteristic of presence, and the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

The characteristic of moments, the characteristic of continuity, the characteristic of illness and so forth, the characteristic of the activity of the mind and mental factors, the characteristic of the attainment and loss of enjoyments, and the characteristic of the dissolution and evolution of the receptacle world.
What is the characteristic of non-existence? It is the perpetual absence of a self or anything belonging to a self within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields at all times.
What is the characteristic of destruction? It is the cessation of conditioned phenomena that have arisen; it is their non-existence after having existed.
What is the characteristic of transformation? It is the alteration of conditioned phenomena; it is their proceeding by way of dissimilarity in their continuity.
What is the characteristic of separation?
It is the loss of mastery over conditioned phenomena or their appropriation by others.
What is the characteristic of proximity?
Present impermanence is that very impermanence which is being experienced at that very moment.
What is the characteristic of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)? It is the impermanence that is yet to come,
which one will inevitably experience.
What is the characteristic of momentariness? It is the non-abiding of conditioned phenomena beyond a single moment.
What is the characteristic of continuity?
It is the non-cessation of the continuity of conditioned phenomena that have arisen and ceased within beginningless saṃskāra.
What are the characteristics of illness and so forth?
They are the timely experience of the four great elements and the transformation of life.
What is the characteristic of the activity of the mind and mental factors?
At times a mind accompanied by passion arises, and at times a mind free from passion arises;

just as there may be a mind with hatred or free from hatred, with delusion or free from delusion, contracted or distracted, depressed or elated, agitated or unagitated, tranquil or untranquil, or concentrated or unconcentrated.
Such is the operation of the mind within saṃsāra.
What is the characteristic of the success and failure of enjoyments?
It is that at the end of successes there is failure and destruction.
What is the characteristic of the dissolution and formation of the receptacle world?
The process of dissolution and evolution is threefold, caused by fire, water, and wind.
The summits of the three types of dissolution are the second, third, and fourth dhyānas respectively.
As for the external celestial palaces within the fourth dhyāna, there is no dissolution or evolution because they lack any external material basis.
Those celestial palaces arise together with those gods and cease together with them; this is called the process of dissolution and evolution (saṃvarta-vivarta).
Furthermore, there are three intermediate kalpas that occur through famine, disease, and weapons.
At the end of these three types of inferior kalpas, there is an exit by means of those weapons and so forth,
when the world-system has dissolved.
The first intermediate kalpa is the period of decrease;
the final intermediate kalpa is the period of increase;
and eighteen intermediate kalpas constitute the periods of both increase and decrease.
In this way, the world-system undergoes dissolution for twenty intermediate kalpas; it undergoes evolution for twenty intermediate kalpas;
and once evolved, it remains for twenty intermediate kalpas.
These eighty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) constitute one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
By means of that reckoning of kalpas, the lifespan of the gods who dwell in the realms of form (rūpadhātu) and formlessness (ārūpyadhātu) is described.
As it has been stated by some:
"Beings fall from that abode due to the exhaustion of their lifespan, or the exhaustion of their merit, or the exhaustion of their karma. In this regard, what is the exhaustion of lifespan?
Death at the proper time;
what is the exhaustion of merit?
It is untimely death and death through demerit.
By which beings are attached to the meditative attainment through its relish;
and due to the exhaustion of merit, they fall away from life.
What is the exhaustion of karma?
Death occurs from the exhaustion of both karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
What is the characteristic of suffering?
It consists of the three types of suffering (*duḥkhatā*), or suffering in eight aspects, or in six aspects.

Suffering has been explained extensively above; that is what is called "suffering. What was stated in the *Pratītyasūtra*—namely, "that which is impermanent is suffering"—is because the characteristic of suffering is discerned in dependence upon a twofold aspect of impermanence.
In dependence upon impermanence consisting in the aspect of arising, the suffering of suffering is discerned;
in dependence upon impermanence consisting in the aspect of passing away, the suffering of change is discerned;
and in dependence upon impermanence consisting in both aspects, the suffering of conditioned formations is discerned.

And thus, with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena and the transformation of conditioned phenomena, it was said by the Blessed One: "Whatever is felt, all that is here included within suffering."

Furthermore, with the intention that among conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), which are subject to the two characteristics of arising and passing away, the eight [factors] beginning with birth are recognized as sufferings, the Buddha taught: "That which is impermanent is suffering.

Moreover, the underlying intention (abhisandhi) here should be understood as follows: suffering, such as birth and so forth, is recognized within impermanent conditioned phenomena; thus, it is in terms of impermanence that they are suffering, not that all conditioned phenomena are themselves suffering.
What is the characteristic of emptiness?
It is the non-existence of that [quality] within those [phenomena].
Emptiness is the observation by way of this method.
Furthermore, among those [factors], there is the existence of the other;
by this method, there is the existence of knowledge as it truly is.
This indeed is called the emptiness of entry.
Knowledge of things as they truly are is the non-erroneous object.
Among those, what is non-existence?
It is the absence of a self, a belonging to a self, or any entity characterized by permanence, stability, immutability, and incorruptibility within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
By this method, their emptiness [is established].
Among them, what is the existence of another?
It is simply selflessness within those very things.
And that which is the non-existence of a self and the existence of non-self is emptiness.
With this in mind, the Blessed One said: "The knowledge of what exists as it really is is existence; the knowledge of what does not exist as it really is is non-existence."
Furthermore, emptiness is indeed threefold:
emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of suchness (*tathābhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of primordial nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
The first is to be understood as the imagined (*parikalpita*).
The third is to be regarded as the perfected nature.

What is the characteristic of non-self? It is the absence of that characteristic of a self— such as it is conceived by one who adheres to the doctrine of a self— within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Based on the absence of the characteristic of a self within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases,
this is called the characteristic of non-self.
It was with this intention that the Blessed One said, "All phenomena are without self."
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One: "All this is not mine; I am not this; this is not my self.
Having understood this as it truly is, it should be seen thus. What is the meaning of that which was said? It was said, "All this is not mine," with reference to external objects.
Why is this so?
Because the characteristic of "mine" is imagined with respect to external objects;
therefore, there is the extraction of "mine."
Regarding internal phenomena, there is the imagined characteristic of self and what belongs to the self;
therefore, there is the extraction of both self and what belongs to the self.
It was previously stated that the characteristic of the moment is impermanent.
How is this known?
Just as the momentariness of the mind and mental factors is established, so too should the momentariness of form and the other aggregates be understood.

This is based on their being appropriated by the mind, based on their sharing the same security and vulnerability as the mind, based on the fact that changes in them correspond to changes in the mind, based on their having the mind as their support, based on their being produced through the sovereignty of the mind, and because they are subject to the power of the mind.
Depending upon [them].

Furthermore, momentariness should be understood to apply to form as well, on account of its being perceived as undergoing absolute transformation, and on account of its inherent perishability once it has arisen, independent of any further causal conditions.
Regarding what was said— that whatever form there is, all that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements— what was intended by that statement?
It was stated with reference to their origination.
The meaning of "derived" (upādāya) is the state of having a single part as its basis.
Furthermore, in whatever aggregate a particular element is perceived, it should be stated that it exists therein:
there is that which consists of one element, there is that which consists of two elements, and so on, up to that which consists of all elements.
Regarding derived matter as well, it should be understood that whatever derived matter is perceived within a particular aggregate exists therein.
Furthermore, regarding what is said—that matter is a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*)—in that context, the atom should be understood as being without a physical body.

However, the establishment of the atom is by means of the analytical division of limits through the intellect; this is for the purpose of breaking down the notion of a solid mass and for the purpose of entering into the perfected nature of the substance within matter.
Furthermore, this suffering is extensive; it is unrefined, refined, both refined and unrefined, and completely refined.

There is that which is moderately refined; there is that which is slightly unrefined; there is that which is more refined; there is that which is most refined; and there is that which is without suffering yet appears as suffering, being the manifestation of great refinement.
What is the extensive suffering that is not attenuated? It is that which belongs to the realm of desire for those who have not accumulated roots of merit.
What is "thoroughly refined"?
It is that very same [state] for those who have already produced the factors conducive to liberation.
What is that which is both refined and unrefined?
It is precisely those same roots of merit planted for the sake of mundane detachment.
What is moderately refined?

It is that of those born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) who have abandoned the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya). What is slightly refined? It is that of those [born in the realm of form] who have not abandoned them.
For those born in the formless realm who have abandoned the factors conducive to liberation.
What is the unsurpassed refinement?
That which belongs to those in training (śaikṣas).
What is the most subtle and refined?
It is the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), which are conditioned by the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
What is that which is not suffering, yet appears as suffering, and is characterized by great austerity?
It is that which exists for Bodhisattvas who have attained the perfections within inconceivable rebirths in existence.
Regarding what was stated— that death is suffering— therein,
death is of three kinds: [death] with a wholesome mind, with an indeterminate mind, and [with an unwholesome mind].
Death with a wholesome state of mind should be understood as occurring when, in a certain mental condition, there is either the strengthening of one's own roots of virtue or the influence of another.

Death with an unwholesome mind should be understood as occurring when the mental state is indeed sharp, either due to the reinforcement of the power of one's own unwholesome roots or through the influence of others.
Death should be understood as occurring when the mind is either clear or unclear, or when it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), being incapable of volitional effort due to the deficiency of both.
For one who has performed virtuous deeds, the lower part of the body becomes cool first.
Furthermore, for one who has performed unwholesome deeds, the upper body becomes cold.
Therein, for one who has performed unwholesome deeds, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests;
it appears like the luster of a black woolen blanket or like the pitch-black darkness of night.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belongs to those who have performed unwholesome deeds— for example, like the appearance of white or the moonlight of a night—
and it pertains to one being reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as to one passing away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
And that mind-made being is also called a *gandharva*;
it remains for at most seven days, or dies in the interim,
and sometimes it turns back.
Remaining there, one accumulates karma and sees beings of a similar class;
wherever one is reborn, one takes on that form and possesses unimpeded movement.
Moving as swiftly as one endowed with supernatural power (*ṛddhimat*), one is nonetheless obstructed at the place of rebirth.
By means of the process of the tilting of a scale, one passes away from the place of birth and takes rebirth;
while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one generates desire for the place of birth,
as well as other afflictions that serve as conditions.
The intermediate state ceases along with passion, and the embryo (kalala) arises together with consciousness.
And that maturation is followed by the manifestation of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), as described in the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) regarding the four modes of birth:
the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), the moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*), and the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*).
(Now, in the first section on the Truths within the *Viniścaya*, the second part:
What is the truth of origination?
It is the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the karma governed by the afflictions.

However, the Blessed One, the Teacher, has designated craving— which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion, and finds delight here and there— as the primary factor in his exposition of the truth of origination.
What is the meaning of preeminence?
It is the meaning of omnipresence.

What is the meaning of "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*)? It is as follows: craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is pervasive with respect to objects, pervasive with respect to states, pervasive with respect to time periods (*adhvan*), pervasive with respect to realms (*dhātu*), pervasive with respect to seeking (*eṣaṇā*), and pervasive with respect to modes (*prakāra*). What is the defilement (*keśa*)?

[It is to be understood] by way of enumeration, by way of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), by way of origination (*utthāna*), by way of object (*ālambana*), by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), by way of synonyms (*paryāya*), by way of misconception (*vipratipatti*), by way of realm (*dhātu*), by way of category (*nikāya*), and by way of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Affliction should also be viewed in this way.
What is enumeration?
There are six or ten afflictions.
What are the six afflictions?
They are attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, and views.
These very [five] become ten through the fivefold division of the aspects of vision.
What is the characteristic?
It is that phenomenon which, as it arises, arises with an unpeaceful characteristic, by means of which there occurs the non-appeasement of the continuity of body and mind;
this is the characteristic of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is arising?
It is when the latent tendency of the afflictions has not been abandoned, an object conducive to the afflictions has come into range,
and improper mental attention is present therein.
In this way, affliction arises; this is called "arising."
What is the object? It is the application of all afflictions.
It has all afflictions as its object and all things that are the basis of afflictions as its object.
Furthermore, with the exception of ignorance, views, and doubt, other afflictions belonging to the desire realm do not have the higher realms as their object.
Afflictions belonging to the higher realms do not have the lower realms as their object.
Because one is free from passion regarding that level,
the affliction that has the truths of cessation and the path as its object is not adhered to by the cessation and the path themselves; rather,
it is said that the conceptual construction of them is its object.
Furthermore, affliction is of two kinds:
that which has a non-substantial object and that which has a substantial object.
What is the object that lacks a real entity? It consists of the views and the mental factors associated with those views.
That which is other than that is called "having a real entity as its object."
What is association?
Attachment is not associated with aversion;
as with aversion, it is also not associated with doubt.
In the remaining cases, application is obtained.
Just as with attachment, so too should aversion be understood.
Repugnance is not associated with attachment, pride, or views.
Pride is not associated with either hostility or doubt.
Ignorance is twofold:
ignorance associated with all the afflictions,
and specific ignorance.
What is the uncommon ignorance?
It is non-knowledge regarding the truths.
View is not associated with hostility or doubt.
The secondary afflictions, such as anger and the rest, do not associate with one another.
Lack of shame and lack of dread are generally associated with all unwholesome states.
Stiffness, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, and heedlessness are associated with every defiled state.
What is a synonym? All afflictions have various meanings and various bases; these are the synonyms:

fetter (*saṃyojana*), bond (*bandhana*), latent tendency (*anuśaya*), secondary affliction (*upakleśa*), envelopment (*paryavasthāna*), flood (*ogha*), yoke (*yoga*), clinging (*upādāna*), and knot (*grantha*).
It is an obscuration, a barrenness, a stain, a disease, a thorn, a possession, misconduct, an influx, an obstacle, a burning fever,
a conflict, a plague, and a blockage.
How many fetters (saṃyojana) are there? What is a fetter? Where does a fetter operate? There are nine fetters:

the fetter of attachment (anunaya), the fetter of aversion (pratigha), the fetter of pride (māna), the fetter of ignorance (avidyā), the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi), the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa), the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā), and the fetter of envy (īrṣyā).
And the fetter of stinginess. What is the fetter of attachment? It is passion for the three realms.
One who is bound by the fetter of attachment does not feel revulsion toward the three realms.
Due to this lack of revulsion, there is the practice of unwholesome states and the non-practice of wholesome states.
Consequently, having brought about suffering in the future, one becomes conjoined with suffering.

(Abhidh-s 45) What is the fetter of repugnance (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)? It is the mind’s malice toward sentient beings, toward suffering, and toward things that are the basis of suffering, but not toward phenomena (*dharma*).

One who is bound by the fetter of aversion does not maintain equanimity toward the objects of aversion. Due to this lack of equanimity, there is the manifestation of unwholesome states and the non-manifestation of wholesome states.
Consequently, when worldly suffering arises in the future, one becomes joined with that suffering.
What is the fetter of pride? It consists of the seven types of pride:
pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," conceit, inferiority pride, and false pride.
What is pride?
It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to those who are inferior," or "I am equal to one who is my equal."
What is excessive pride (*atimāna*)?
It is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am superior to my equal," or "I am equal to one who is superior.
What is pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*)?

What is the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to one who is superior. What is the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*)? It is that inflation of the mind arising from the adherence to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as being a self or belonging to a self.

What is overweening pride (*abhimāna*)? It is the inflation of the mind that thinks, "I have attained it," regarding a superior, distinguished realization that has not actually been attained. What is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*)?
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)? It is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I am only slightly inferior" to one who is vastly superior. What is pride of self (*abhimāna*)?
It is the inflation of the mind thinking, "I possess qualities" when one actually possesses no qualities.
One who is bound by the fetter of pride does not perceive "self" and "what belongs to self.
Due to this non-perception, there arises the grasping of self and what belongs to self, which consists in the manifestation of unwholesome states and the non-manifestation of wholesome states.
Consequently, when suffering is produced in the future, one becomes conjoined with that suffering.
What is the fetter of ignorance?
It is non-knowledge regarding the three realms.
One who is associated with the fetter of ignorance does not correctly discern the phenomena of suffering or the phenomena of their origin.
Through lack of resolute determination, there is the manifestation of the unwholesome and the non-manifestation of the wholesome;
by that means, one becomes joined with suffering when worldly suffering arises in the future.
What is the fetter of views? It consists of three views:
the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes, and false view.

One who is fettered by the fetter of views adheres to a false means of deliverance and to remorse that is merely imagined during their search. Through this adherence to a false means of deliverance, there occurs the practice of unwholesome states and the non-practice of wholesome states.
Consequently, when worldly suffering arises in the future, one becomes joined with suffering.
What is the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
It is the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).
One who is bound by the fetter of grasping imagines and adheres to a false means of deliverance.
Through adherence to false means of deliverance, there is the practice of unwholesome states and the non-practice of wholesome states;
by this, one is joined with suffering when worldly suffering arises in the future.
What is the fetter of doubt?
It is indecision regarding the truths.
One who is conjoined with the fetter of doubt doubts the Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and does not fully embrace the Triple Gem.
Through the non-practice of the Three Jewels, there occurs the practice of the unwholesome and the non-practice of the wholesome;
by means of that, one is joined with suffering when worldly suffering arises in the future.
What is the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
It is a state of mental resentment toward the excellence of others, produced by the intolerance of one who is attached to gain and honor.
One who is bound by the fetter of envy pursues gain and honor and does not hold the Dharma in high regard.
Through the prioritization of gain and honor, there is the practice of unwholesome states and the non-practice of wholesome states;
by means of that, one becomes joined with suffering when worldly suffering arises in the future.
What is the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*)?
It is the mind’s attachment to requisites in one who is obsessed with gain and honor.
One who is conjoined with the fetter of avarice pursues accumulation and does not respect the state of renunciation.
Through attachment to accumulation, there is the manifestation of unwholesome states and the non-manifestation of wholesome states;
by means of that, one is joined with suffering in the future upon the production of worldly suffering.
Bondage is threefold:
the bondage of attachment, the bondage of aversion, and the bondage of delusion.
By the bondage of attachment, sentient beings are bound to the suffering of change.
By the bond of hatred, sentient beings are bound to the suffering of suffering;
by the bond of delusion, sentient beings are bound to the suffering of conditioned formations.
Furthermore, depending on attachment, hatred, and delusion, one does not attain mastery over wholesome conduct.
Therefore, it is called bondage.
There are seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):

the latent disposition of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), the latent disposition of aversion (*pratigha*), the latent disposition of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*), the latent disposition of pride (*māna*), the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā*), the latent disposition of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the latent disposition of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
What is the latent disposition of sensual desire?
The depravity belonging to the side of sensual desire.
What is the latent tendency of aversion?
It is the functional rigidity belonging to the side of aversion.
What is the latent tendency of attachment to existence?
It is the functional rigidity belonging to the category of attachment to the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the latent tendency of pride? It is the functional rigidity belonging to the category of pride.
What is the latent tendency of ignorance? It is the functional rigidity belonging to the side of ignorance.
What is the latent tendency of views?
It is the functional rigidity associated with the side of views.
What is the latent tendency of doubt?
It is the functional rigidity belonging to the side of doubt.

For one who has not desisted from the quest for sensual pleasures, the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion persist. For one who has not desisted from the quest for existence, the latent tendency of craving for existence persists.
For one who has not desisted from the quest for a false holy life, the latent tendencies of pride, ignorance, views, and doubt persist.
Those beings obtain inferior remedies; pride and conceit arise, as does delusion regarding the Noble Truths.

They falsely imagine what is not liberation to be liberation and what is not the means to liberation to be the means to liberation; they harbor indecision and doubt regarding the Buddha’s teaching, the Dharma, and the Vinaya.
Those which are afflictions (*kleśa*) are also secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
but there are secondary afflictions that are not afflictions.
Excluding the afflictions themselves, they are all other defiled mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
What, then, is that?

It is any afflicted mental factor (caitasika-dharma) comprised within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), excluding the six afflictions beginning with attachment, such as anger and the like.
Furthermore, attachment, aversion, and delusion are also called secondary afflictions (upakleśa).

Because they cause defilement in the mind, but not dispassion, nor liberation, nor the abandonment of hindrances, they are called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*). Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "For a long time, passion, hatred, and delusion have defiled, distracted, and thoroughly afflicted your minds."
There are eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
torpor, drowsiness, restlessness, regret, envy, avarice, lack of shame, and lack of dread.
They are called envelopments because they repeatedly and intensely shroud the mind with agitation.
