As it is said in the Sūtra: "He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and strives with the mind.
By such phrases as these, the cultivation of the basis of energy (*vīryāśraya-bhāvanā*) is elucidated therein.
The basis is desire;
vigor is exertion.
One generates desire for the mental attentions toward the signs of calm abiding, exertion, and equanimity.
One initiates vigor for the removal of lethargy and excitement; thus, immediately thereafter, it is said that one "upholds" and "exerts" the mind.
What is the fruit of cultivation?
The complete abandonment of all adverse factors, the attainment of the remedies, and the increase of those remedies.
That is called the fruit of cultivation.
What is the object of the four bases of psychic power?
It is whatever task is to be performed by means of perfected concentration.
What is its intrinsic nature?
It is meditative concentration.
What is the companion?
It is desire, vigor, mind, and investigation, as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with them.
What is concentration through desire? It is that which, having relied upon earnest application, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind.
What is the concentration of vigor? It is that which, by means of continuous application, touches one-pointedness of mind.
What is mental concentration?
It is the touching of one-pointedness of mind by means of its own natural flow, having relied upon the prior cultivation of concentration.
What is the concentration of investigation?
Having relied upon hearing the Dharma of the teaching and having applied individual analytical discernment, one touches one-pointedness of mind.
Furthermore, concentration through desire is that by which, generating desire, one touches one-pointedness of mind.
Concentration through vigor is that one-pointedness of mind which vigor, having overcome the Māras, attains.
Concentration of mind is that by which, applying the mind, one touches the one-pointedness of the mind.
The concentration of investigation is that by which, uplifting the mind, one touches one-pointedness of mind.
What is cultivation?
It is the practice of the eight formative forces of abandonment.
What are the eight?
Zeal, exertion, faith, serenity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity—
these eight, in brief, are subsumed under four categories:
those consisting of exertion, those that are supportive, those that are binding, and those that are remedial.
Furthermore, the cultivation of desire, energy, mind, and investigation is twofold:
the cultivation of avoiding the causes of contraction and distraction, and the cultivation conducive to the basis of both non-depression and non-distraction.
What is the fruit?

It is the mastery of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) according to one's action through the cultivation of wholesome concentration; it is the manifestation of supernormal knowledges according to one's intention.

Furthermore, it consists in the realization, attainment, adaptability, mastery, and functional activity regarding various phenomena; it is the accomplishment of various kinds of objects such as miracles (*ṛddhi*) at will, and the production of higher qualities.
(Abhidh-s 74) What is the object of the five faculties?
It is the four noble truths.
What is its intrinsic nature?
It consists of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
What is the companion?
It consists of the mind and mental factors associated with it.
What is cultivation? It is the cultivation of application consisting in the arousal of firm conviction regarding the truths by means of the faculty of faith;

and it is the cultivation of application consisting in the arousal of exertion for the sake of full awakening regarding the truths by one who has already produced firm conviction by means of the faculty of vigor.

Through the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), for one who has initiated vigor regarding the truths, there is the cultivation of the application that gives rise to the non-forgetting of phenomena through the conjunction with mindfulness. Through the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), for one whose mindfulness is conjoined with the truths, there is the cultivation of the application that gives rise to one-pointedness of mind.
Through the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), for one whose mind is concentrated upon the truths, there is the cultivation of the application that gives rise to discernment.
What is the fruit of cultivation?

It is the production of the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), arising from the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) and through the refinement of the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summits" (*mūrdhan*).

As it is with the five faculties, so it is with the five powers. Their distinction is this: because they have eradicated their opposing factors and obstacles and are no longer subject to being overwhelmed, they are called "powers."
What is the object of the seven factors of enlightenment?
It is the suchness of the four noble truths. What is their intrinsic nature?
Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity.
Mindfulness is the factor of support;
investigation of phenomena is the factor of essential nature;
and vigor is the factor of departure.
Joy is the limb of benefit;
serenity,
concentration, and equanimity are the limbs of non-affliction.
By way of non-affliction, by way of being the basis of non-affliction, and by way of having non-affliction as its intrinsic nature.
What is the companion? It consists of those mental factors associated with it that depend upon it.
What is cultivation?
It is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
As it is with the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, so it is for all others up to the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity.
By these four phrases, the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) having the four truths as their respective objects is elucidated. What is the fruit of this cultivation?
It is the abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa) to be abandoned by seeing.
What is the object of the eight limbs of the noble path?
It is the suchness of the four noble truths at a subsequent time.
What is its intrinsic nature?
It consists of right view, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Right view is the limb of discernment;
right resolve is the limb of causing others to attain [the goal];
and right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the limbs of inspiring confidence in others.

Right effort is the limb for purifying the obscuration of the afflictions, by means of the purity of view, conduct, and livelihood. Right concentration is the limb for purifying the obscuration of the distinguished qualities.
What is the associate?
It consists of the mental states and mental factors associated with it.
What is cultivation?
Cultivation, however, is like that of the factors of enlightenment.
What is the fruit of cultivation?

It is discernment, bringing [the goal] to others, inspiring confidence in others, and the purification of the obscuration of afflictions, the purification of the obscuration of secondary afflictions, and the purification of the obscuration of extraordinary qualities.
What are the four modes of practice?

The painful practice with slow direct knowledge; the painful practice with quick direct knowledge; the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge; and the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
The first is for those of dull faculties who have not attained the fundamental dhyānas; the second is for those of sharp faculties who have not attained the fundamental dhyānas;
the third is for those of dull faculties who have attained the fundamental dhyānas.
The fourth [alternative] refers to those of sharp faculties who have attained the fundamental dhyāna.
What are the four bases of dharma? They are: non-attachment and non-hatred; right mindfulness and right concentration;
and the purification of the training in higher ethics through non-attachment and non-hatred.
For those who possess right mindfulness, there is the purification of the training in higher mind;
for those who possess right concentration, there is the purification of the training in higher wisdom.
What is śamatha?

It is the binding of the mind internally, its placing, its continuous placing, its thorough placing, its close placing, its taming, its pacifying, its complete pacifying, its unification, and its concentration.

What is insight (vipaśyanā)? It is that which discriminates, thoroughly discriminates, investigates, and examines phenomena, by way of counteracting desire, by way of the signs of depravity and fetters, by way of the overcoming of desires, by way of error, and by way of establishing a mind free from error.
Furthermore, based upon calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), there are four types of paths.
One person attains calm abiding but not insight;
relying on that type of calm abiding, they enter into insight.

One person attains insight (vipaśyanā) but not tranquility (śamatha); relying on that kind of insight, they cultivate the development of tranquility. Another person attains neither tranquility nor insight.
Because one whose mind is connected to that [object] removes both laxity and excitement, there is the cultivation of both paths simultaneously.
A certain person attains both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*);
for him, who is endowed with the path of both calm abiding and insight, there is an equal, simultaneous engagement.
There are three faculties:
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
It is the faculty [present] during the path of preparation and during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing.
What is the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*)?
It is that faculty which exists throughout the entire path of training (*śaikṣamārga*) subsequent to the sixteenth moment of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What is the faculty of one who has already known?
It is the faculty that exists on the path of no-more-learning.

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, even the wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) undergo cultivation,
because mastery (*vibhutva*) is attained over them.

Just as the wholesome roots of the desire realm undergo cultivation for those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, so too do the wholesome roots of the lower levels undergo cultivation on the path of cultivation for all those belonging to the higher levels.
They proceed to cultivation through the attainment of mastery over them.
What is the path of culmination?
It is the diamond-like samādhi,
because of the subsiding of all dysfunctions, the abandonment of all fetters, and the attainment of all disjunctions.

Immediately following that, there is the uninterrupted progression of the basis: the attainment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
What are the ten?
They are the right view of one beyond training, up to the right concentration of one beyond training, the right liberation of one beyond training, and the right knowledge of one beyond training.
These and other such factors are called the path of culmination.
What are all the dysfunctions? Briefly, there are twenty-four:
namely, the pervasive dysfunction of verbal expression, the dysfunction of sensation, the dysfunction of afflictions, and the dysfunction of karma.

The depravity of maturation; the depravity of the obscuration of afflictions; the depravity of the obscuration of karma; the depravity of the obscuration of maturation; the depravity of the hindrances;
the depravity of discursive thought; the depravity of food; the depravity of sexual intercourse; the depravity of sleep; the depravity of illness;
the depravity of old age; the depravity of death; the depravity of fatigue; and the depravity of firmness.
Coarse dysfunction, middling dysfunction, subtle dysfunction, dysfunction that is an obstruction to meditative attainment, and dysfunction that is an obstruction to the knowable.
What is conjunction?
It is the representation of the attainment of conjunction within those things accumulated by corruption.
What is dissociation?
It is the representation that there is the attainment of dissociation from those states that are agitated by depravity.
What is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)?

It is the concentration belonging to one who has entered the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), occurring in the stage of the path for abandoning the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*). It is comprised either within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) or the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
That which is comprised within the path of preparation is, thereafter, incapable of being obscured by any obscurations and is the breaker of all obscurations.

The inclusion within the path of immediate succession (ānantaryamārga) is that immediately following which the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) arise;
and that concentration is uninterrupted, firm, of a single flavor, and all-pervading.

To illustrate this point, the Blessed One said: "It is just as if there were a great mountain of solid rock—unbroken, without fissures, without cavities, a single solid mass, well-compacted, and unshakable by the winds from the ten directions."
What is the uninterrupted transformation of the basis?
For one who has attained the path of no-more-learning, there is a threefold transformation of the basis.
What are the three?
The non-functioning of the basis of the mind, the non-functioning of the basis of the noble ones, and the non-functioning of the basis of coarse wickedness.

What is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna)? It is the knowledge that is obtained through the destruction of its cause, or that which has the destruction [of defilements] as its object or focal point.
What is the knowledge of non-arising?
It is the knowledge obtained through the abandonment of the fruit, or that which has as its object and support the non-arising of the fruit.

The ten qualities of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dharma), however, should be understood with reference to the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-skandha), the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha) of those beyond training.
Likewise, there are four distinct aspects of the truth of the path (mārga-satya):

the characteristic of the path (mārga-lakṣaṇa), the characteristic of the method (nyāya-lakṣaṇa), the characteristic of the practice (pratipad-lakṣaṇa), and the characteristic of leading to deliverance (nairyāṇika-lakṣaṇa).
On what basis is the characteristic of the path established?
On the basis of its being the thorough investigation of the meaning of reality.
On what basis is the definition of "reasoning" (nyāya) established?
It is established on the basis of being an antidote to the afflictions (kleśa).
On what basis is it the characteristic of practice?
On the basis of its accomplishing the non-perversion of the mind.
On what basis is the characteristic of leading to liberation established?
It is established on the basis of the state of being the vehicle to the eternal.
Regarding the truths, there are sixteen aspects, both mundane and supramundane.
What is the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane?

It is the distinction based on the nature of entering unskillfully or skillfully into the object of knowledge; the distinction based on the nature of being with obscurations or without obscurations; and the distinction based on the nature of being with conceptualization or without conceptualization.
For what reason are there sixteen mundane aspects, such as impermanence and suffering, regarding the truths?
It is because of the non-penetration of the Tathāgata, because of the latent tendencies of the afflictions, and because of conceptual proliferation by way of verbal expression.
The supramundane aspects are the opposite of those.

When one operates within the supramundane aspects, one sees the meaning of impermanence directly and experiences it, but one does not see impermanence by way of the proliferation of verbal expression.
Just as the aspect of impermanence relates to the meaning of impermanence, so too should the remaining aspects be understood in relation to their respective meanings, as appropriate.
(Abhidh-s 78) Now, in the *Viniścaya*, this is the second part, the section on the determination of phenomena (*dharmapariccheda*).
What is the determination of phenomena (*dharmaviniścaya*)?
The Noble Teaching is the Dharma consisting of twelve branches.
What are the twelve branches?
They are: Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa.
1. What is a sūtra? It is that which is spoken in prose by way of indicating a intended meaning.
Perceiving ten benefits, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by way of indication; he establishes it easily and teaches it easily.

The listener also grasps [the teaching] easily through reverence for the Dharma; he quickly fulfills the accumulations for awakening and swiftly penetrates the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). He attains unwavering confidence in the Buddha, and he attains unwavering confidence in the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He touches the supreme dwelling in happiness in this very life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra).
Through the definitive resolution of discussion, he delights the minds of the virtuous;
he is reckoned as a wise man, indeed a wise man.
2. What is *geya*?
It is that which is sung in verse either in the midst or at the end of the sūtras;
or it is that which explains a meaning not explicitly determined in the sūtras.
Therefore, it is called "geya" (song).
3. What is exposition (vyākaraṇa)?

It is the exposition of the distinctions regarding the attainment and arising of noble disciples (ārya-śrāvaka) who have passed away in the past and transcended those [worldly] states. Furthermore, it is the clarification of the meaning as it has been determined in the sūtras.
Because it is explained through the disclosure of the underlying intention.
4. What is a verse (*gāthā*)? It is taught in the sūtras by means of metrical feet; it consists of two lines, three lines, four lines, five lines, or six lines.
5. What is an *udāna*?
It is that which has been uttered at times by the Tathāgata in the sūtras when he was filled with joy.
6. What is the *nidāna*? It is that which is spoken when questioned, or that which includes the origin story (*sotpattika*) concerning the establishment of a training rule (*śikṣāprajñapti*).
For this reason also.
7. What is an *avadāna*?
It is that which is spoken in the sūtras together with an illustrative example.
8. What is an *itivṛttaka*?
It is that which teaches the former worldly conduct of the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*).
9. What is a jātaka? It is that which teaches events connected with the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
10. What is the Vaipulya? It is that which is spoken in connection with the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
That which is called *vaipulya* is also called *vaidalya* and is also called *vaitulya*. For what reason is it called *vaipulya*?
Because it is the basis for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, and because it is the teaching of the vast and profound Dharma.
For what purpose is it called Vaidalya? Because it shatters all obscurations.
For what purpose is it called "ineffable" (vaitulya)? Because there is no possibility of weighing the qualities of its analogies.
11. What is the marvelous quality (adbhutadharma)?
It is that wherein the supreme, marvelous, and extraordinary qualities of the disciples, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are taught.
12. What is instruction (*upadeśa*)?
It is the unerring explanation of all the profound and hidden characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the twelvefold limbs of the noble teachings, beginning with the discourses (*sūtra*), are subsumed within the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Which three?
The Sūtra Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka, and the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
These, moreover, are of two kinds.
There is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, and udāna—these five are included within the Sūtra-piṭaka of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, and jātaka—these four, along with their attendants, are included within the Vinaya-piṭaka of both piṭakas.
The *Vaipulya* and the *Adbhutadharma*—these two are included within the Sūtra Piṭaka of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The *Upadeśa* alone is included within the Abhidharma Piṭaka of both the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva Piṭakas.
On what basis is the Tathāgata’s establishment of the three Piṭakas?
The establishment of the Sūtra Piṭaka is based on the desire to provide an antidote for the secondary affliction of doubt.
The establishment of the Vinaya Piṭaka is based on the desire to provide an antidote for the secondary affliction of devotion to the two extremes.
The establishment of the Abhidharma Piṭaka is based on the desire to provide an antidote for the secondary affliction of clinging to one's own views.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established based on the desire for proficiency in the three trainings;
the Vinaya Piṭaka is established based on the desire for the accomplishment of the training in higher ethics and the training in higher mind;
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established based on the desire for the accomplishment of the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established based on the desire for the correct understanding of the meaning of the Dharma;
the Vinaya Piṭaka is established based on being the basis for the realization of the Dharma and its meaning;
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established based on being the support for the blissful dwelling in the enjoyment of the Dharma through the definitive resolution of discussions among the wise.
Of what is this Dharma, comprised within the three baskets (piṭaka), the domain?
It is the domain of the mental states and mental factors consisting of those arisen from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "The mental states and mental factors have an object, possess an aspect, have a basis, and are associated.
Among these, what is their object in this dharma?
It is the Sūtras and so forth.
What is the aspect?
It consists of the aggregates and so forth, as well as the objects associated with them.
What is the basis?
It is the representation of another, mindfulness, and habitual tendencies.

What is association (*saṃprayoga*)? It is the simultaneous engagement [of mental factors] with respect to an object by means of their respective modes (*ākāra*), through their state of mutual assistance.
Regarding the Dharma, what is the classification of the objects of focus?
In brief, it is explained as being fourfold:
the pervasive object of focus, the object of focus for purifying conduct, the object of focus for skillfulness, and the object of focus for purifying afflictions.
Furthermore, the pervasive object of focus (vyāpyālambana) is fourfold:

the object of focus that is a conceptual reflection (savikalpapratibimbālambana), the object of focus that is a non-conceptual reflection (nirvikalpaprativimbālambana), the object of focus that is the limit of things (vastuparyantālambana), and the object of focus that is the perfection of what is to be done (kāryapariniṣpattyālambana).
What is the object that is a conceptual reflection?
It is that which is the object of the domain of calm abiding and insight through mental attention consisting of resolute belief.
What is the object of focus consisting of a non-conceptual reflection?
It is that which, through mental attention directed toward reality, serves as the object of the domain of calm abiding and special insight.
What is the object that is the limit of things?
It is the state of the exhaustion of all phenomena and their state of being as they truly are.
What is the nature of exhaustion? It consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*)?

It consists of the four noble truths in their sixteen aspects: that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-self, and that nirvāṇa is peace; as well as emptiness, the wishless, and the signless.
What is the objective support for the fulfillment of the task?
It is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
This transformation of the basis is inconceivable.
Among the sixteen aspects, how many aspects are subsumed within emptiness? Two.
How many aspects are subsumed within the wishless?
Six.
How many aspects are included in the signless? Eight.
(Abhidh-s 81)
The object for purifying conduct is fivefold:
for those whose temperament is dominated by attachment, the object is the sphere of the foul;
for those whose temperament is dominated by aversion, the object is the cultivation of compassion.
For those whose conduct is dominated by delusion, the object of focus is the conditionality of the group [of elements] as dependent origination;

for those whose conduct is dominated by intoxication and pride, the object of focus is the analysis of the elements; for those whose conduct is dominated by discursive thought, the object of focus is mindfulness that neither enters nor turns back.
Skillfulness regarding the focal object is fivefold:

skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense-bases, skillfulness regarding dependent origination, and skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible.
Through skill in the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, what object does one perceive?
One perceives skill in dependent origination regarding the objects of knowledge.
What is the distinction between skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*) and skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*)?

That phenomena flow forth from phenomena—that their arising is neither without cause nor from discordant causes—this is skill in dependent origination. That the arising of experience occurs in accordance with the correspondence between cause and fruit—this is skill in the possible and the impossible.
What is the object for the purification of afflictions?
It is the coarseness of the lower stages, the tranquility of the higher stages, suchness, and the four noble truths.
These are called the objects for the purification of afflictions.
In that regard, by how many reasonings is it investigated by one who desires to examine the Dharma? It is investigated by four reasonings:
the reasoning of dependence, the reasoning of causal efficiency, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena.
What is the principle of dependence?
It is the dependence upon conditions for the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). What is the principle of cause and effect?
The respective causes and effects of phenomena that possess distinct characteristics.
What is the reasoning that establishes through proof?
It is the teaching of the matter to be proven, for the sake of establishing it through proof, in a manner not contradicted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What is the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*)?

It is the perfection of the nature of phenomena as it exists within all things—both those with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—from beginningless time. That is the nature of phenomena.
Thus is the investigation into phenomena.
Regarding phenomena (*dharmas*), what investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) are possible? Four investigations are possible:

the investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*), the investigation of things (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*), the investigation of designations of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*), and the investigation of designations of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*).
What is the investigation of names? It is the discernment that, among phenomena, the intrinsic characteristic of the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes is unestablished.
What is the investigation of things? It is the analytical examination that the specific characteristics of phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—are indeed unestablished.
What is the investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature?

It is the discernment that, regarding the relationship between the designator and the designated among phenomena, [everything] is merely a designation of intrinsic nature serving as the basis for conventional expression.
What is the investigation into the designation of specificities?
It is the discernment that, regarding the relationship between the designator and the designated among phenomena, the cause for conventional usage is merely the designation of specificities.
Thus is the cultivation of the search for the Dharma.
What kinds of thorough cognitions of phenomena as they truly are (yathābhūtaparijñāna) arise? There are four thorough cognitions of phenomena as they truly are:

the thorough cognition of phenomena as they truly are through the investigation of names, the thorough cognition of phenomena as they truly are through the investigation of things, the thorough cognition of phenomena as they truly are through the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature, and the thorough cognition of phenomena as they truly are through the investigation of the designation of specific qualities.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*):
what is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is through the investigation of names?
It is the knowledge of the non-apprehension of the name of reality as it is.
What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is, sought through the investigation of objects?
It is the knowledge that the characteristics of objects are not perceived as they truly are.
What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is, which is sought through the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature?
It is the knowledge that the substantial intrinsic nature of things is not apprehended as it truly is.
What is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, sought through the designation of specific distinctions?
It is the knowledge that does not perceive any substantial distinction in things as they truly are.
What is to be known as the stage of yoga for one who relies on the Dharma and is engaged in meditative concentration?
There are five aspects:
the support, the placement, the mirror, the light, and the basis.
What is the support?
It is the great learning regarding the noble truths, such as the "heat" stage and others, for one who has accumulated the equipment for enlightenment.
What is application?
It is appropriate mental attention directed toward that object.
What is the mirror-like [samādhi]? It is the samādhi that has that as its object and possesses signs.
What is illumination?
It is the knowledge of the non-apprehension of the apprehended and the apprehender.
With reference to this, it was well said by the Blessed Buddha: "The Bodhisattva, concentrated in meditative absorption, beholding the mind as a reflection,
turns away from the perception of external objects and maintains the perception of its own nature."
Thus, with his mind established in the self, he should realize the non-existence of the object of apprehension;
thereafter, he realizes the non-existence of the subject of apprehension, and from that, he touches upon non-apprehension.
(Abhidh-s 83)
What is the basis?
It is the revolution of the basis.
How does one become skilled in the teachings regarding phenomena?
By means of extensive learning.
How does one become skilled in meaning?
By means of knowing the characteristics within the Abhidharma and the Abhivinaya.
How is one skilled in phonemes?
By virtue of knowing the phonemes of one's own etymological explanations.
How does one become skilled in etymological interpretation? By not adhering to the regional etymologies of "self" and "mine," while nevertheless maintaining knowledge of conventional usage.
How does one become skilled in the connection between the past limit and the future limit?
It is by taking up [the teaching] in the past limit and, based upon that, attaining liberation in the future limit.
How does one become a dweller in the Dharma among the dharmas?
One does not become a dweller in the Dharma by means of the application of hearing and reflection alone, without having recourse to cultivation;
nor does one become a dweller in the Dharma by means of the application of cultivation alone, without having recourse to hearing and reflection.
Having relied upon both, through dwelling in both, one becomes a dweller in the Dharma.
That which consists of hearing is to be understood through the acts of grasping, reciting, and teaching.
That which consists of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya) is to be understood by way of both application to meditative concentration (samādhi-prayoga) and lack of contentment (asantuṣṭi).
Application should be understood by way of constant and respectful application, as well as by way of non-erroneous application.
Lack of contentment is to be understood through the application of higher tranquility that has not yet been tasted.
For what reason is the Vaipulya called the Bodhisattvas’ Piṭaka of the Perfections?

It is because it provides a teaching on the enumeration of the perfections, a teaching on their characteristics, a teaching on their sequence, a teaching on their etymologies, a teaching on their cultivation, a teaching on their classifications, and a teaching on their synthesis.
Based on the exposition of the opposing factors, based on the exposition of the description of qualities, and based on their mutual determination.
For what reason is the Vaipulya taught as being vast and profound?
It is because omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) possesses such vastness and profundity.
For what reason do some beings lack conviction in the vastness and profundity of the Vaipulya and become terrified?
It is because they are devoid of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
On account of not having planted roots of merit and on account of being under the influence of evil friends.
For what reason do some beings have faith in the Vaipulya? Even though they have faith, they do not attain deliverance because they remain fixed in their own adherence to views.

And it was with reference to this that the Blessed One said in the *Mahādharmādarśa* Dharma-discourse: "For a bodhisattva who investigates phenomena according to the letter without applying correct reasoning, twenty-eight false views arise.
What are the twenty-eight false views?

They are: the view of signs (*nimittadṛṣṭi*), the view of the denial of designation (*prajñaptyapavādadṛṣṭi*), the view of the denial of conceptual construction (*parikalpāpavādadṛṣṭi*), the view of the denial of reality (*tattvāpavādadṛṣṭi*), and the view of grasping (*parigrahadṛṣṭi*)."

The view of transformation, the view of faultlessness, the view of escape, the view of contempt, the view of provocation, the perverted view, the view of production, the view of non-acceptance, the view of a crooked path, the view of honor, the view of stubborn delusion, the root view, the view of seeing what is not seen, the view of rejecting application, and the view of non-emancipation; these constitute the accumulation of obscurations.
The view that produces demerit, the view of futility, the view that should be suppressed, the view of false accusation, the view of the unspeakable, the great view, and the view of overweening pride.

Regarding what was stated in the Vaipulya that "all phenomena are without intrinsic nature," what is the underlying intention? It is based on their lack of existence by themselves, their lack of existence through their own self-nature, and the fact that their essence is not established in its own being.
Because it is devoid of grasping, and because it is characterized by the absence of defining marks, like the seizing of a child.

Furthermore, what is the underlying intention [behind the teaching] that [all phenomena] are unarisen, unceasing, quiescent from the beginning, and naturally in a state of parinirvāṇa— by relying on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics regarding the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), by relying on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising regarding the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), and by relying on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate regarding the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva)?
Just as they are without intrinsic nature, so they are unarisen;
just as they are unarisen, so they are unceasing;
and just as they are both unarisen and unceasing, so they are primordially quiescent.
Just as they are primordially peaceful, so too are they naturally parinirvāṇized.
Furthermore, there are four intentions by which the intention of the Tathāgatas in the Vaipulya [sūtras] is to be understood:
the intention of equality, the intention of another time, the intention of another meaning, and the intention regarding the disposition of individuals.
(Abhidh-s 85) There are four intentions (*abhisandhi*) which are to be understood as the intentions of the Tathāgatas in the Vaipulya [sūtras]:

the intention of introduction (*avatāraṇābhisandhi*), the intention of characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*), the intention of counteraction (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*), and the intention of transformation (*pariṇāmanābhisandhi*).
How is a bodhisattva skilled in the dharma-samādhi of the Vaipulya to be understood?
By five reasons:
at every moment, he dissolves the basis of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*).
He attains a delight in the garden of the Dharma that is free from the perception of diversity;
he perceives the illumination of the Dharma as immeasurable and of an undifferentiated form;
and signs conducive to purification, which are non-conceptual, manifest for him.
And for the sake of the fulfillment and perfection of the *dharmakāya*, one undertakes an ever-higher appropriation consisting of causes.
In this regard, it is shown that within the fivefold cultivation, a fivefold fruit is produced.

The fivefold cultivation consists of: mixed cultivation (*saṃbhinnabhāvanā*), signless cultivation (*animittabhāvanā*), effortless cultivation (*anābhogabhāvanā*), refined cultivation (*uttaptabhāvanā*), and that which resembles transformation (*parivṛttinibha*).
Cultivation is according to the sequence.

For what reason is the Vaipulya Dharma to be honored with incense, garlands, and so forth, whereas the Śrāvaka Dharma is not? It is because the former serves as the basis for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
The third compendium in the Abhidharmasamuccaya, titled "The Determination of Dharmas."
(From the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*, in the *Viniścaya* [Section on Determination], in the third chapter on "Attainment" (*prāpti*), the first part:
What is the determination of attainment?
Briefly, it is of two kinds.
It should be understood by way of the establishment of persons and by way of the establishment of clear realization.
(Abhidh-s 86) What is the classification of persons (*pudgala*)?
In brief, it is of seven kinds.

[The classification is] by way of the distinction of diseases and conduct, the distinction of departure, the distinction of support, the distinction of application, the distinction of fruit, the distinction of elements, and the distinction of practice.
What is the classification according to temperament and conduct?
It is sevenfold:

the person of lustful temperament, the person of hateful temperament, the person of deluded temperament, the person of proud temperament, the person of discursive temperament, the person of balanced temperament, and the person of mild-defilement temperament. This is the classification of persons.
What is the classification of the means of deliverance?
It is threefold:

the person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, the person belonging to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, and the person belonging to the Great Vehicle. This is the classification of persons.
What is the classification of the basis?
It is threefold:

the person who has not accumulated the provisions, the person who has both accumulated and not accumulated the provisions, and the person who has accumulated the provisions. This is the classification of persons.
What is the classification by way of application?
It is the classification of persons into those who follow through faith and those who follow through the Dharma.
What is the classification of the fruits?
It is twenty-sevenfold:
one liberated through faith, one who has attained vision, a body-witness, one liberated through wisdom, one liberated both ways, and those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry.

The stream-enterer; the one practicing for the fruit of once-returning; the once-returner; the one practicing for the fruit of non-returning; the non-returner; the one practicing for the fruit of arhatship; the arhat; the one who has seven births at most; the one who goes from family to family; the one with only one interval; the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion; the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion; and the one who flows upwards.

The classification of persons consists of: the Arhat of the nature of falling away, the Arhat of the nature of volition, the Arhat of the nature of guarding, the Arhat who is steadfast and unshakable, the Arhat of the nature of penetration, and the Arhat of the immovable nature.
What is the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*)?

It consists of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the one in training (*śaikṣa*), and the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). Likewise, there are three types [of beings] belonging to the desire realm, the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).

The classification of persons consists of: a bodhisattva belonging to the desire realm and a bodhisattva belonging to the form realm; a pratyekabuddha belonging to the desire realm; and the inconceivable Tathāgata.
What is the classification of conduct?
Briefly, it is fivefold:

the bodhisattva who practices through resolute belief, the bodhisattva who practices through superior intention, the bodhisattva who practices with signs, the bodhisattva who practices without signs, and the bodhisattva who practices without effortful construction.
Who is the person of passionate temperament?
One who possesses intense and extensive passion.
Likewise, persons of hateful temperament, deluded temperament, proud temperament, and discursive temperament are distinguished by their intensity and extensiveness.
What is the person whose conduct consists of equal proportions?
Affliction in its natural state.
What is a person whose conduct is characterized by little passion?
It is one whose afflictions are naturally very slight.
What is a person belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas?
It is one who, whether in meditative absorption or not, dwells in the nature of a śrāvaka; who by nature has dull faculties; who is resolved upon his own liberation;
whose intention is liberated through the cultivation of detachment; and who, relying on the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, applies himself to the cultivation of vigor.
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma reaches the end of suffering.
What is a person belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas?
It is one who, whether in meditative equipoise or not, dwells in the nature of a pratyekabuddha; who is by nature of middling faculties;
who has made a vow for his own liberation; whose intention is liberated through the cultivation of detachment; and whose intention for awakening is attained through solitary cultivation.

Relying on the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, through the cultivation of vigor, practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma— whether one has not previously produced the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) or has previously produced them, whether one has not previously attained the fruit or is a worldly person in a Buddha-less age— one brings the Noble Path face-to-face through internal volition; such a Pratyekajina, who is like the horn of a rhinoceros and dwells alone, or one who moves in a group, reaches the end of suffering.
Who is the person belonging to the Mahāyāna?

It is one who, whether in meditative equipoise or not, dwells in the true nature of a bodhisattva; who by nature possesses sharp faculties; who has made a vow for the liberation of all sentient beings; whose inclination is toward non-abiding nirvāṇa; and who, relying upon the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, practices in accordance with the Dharma through the cultivation of vigor.
He brings sentient beings to maturity, cultivates the pure stage of a Buddha, receives a prophecy, and realizes perfect enlightenment.

What is the person who has not accumulated the equipment? It is one who, having taken as an object the Dharma dominated by the Truths, has produced only a weak degree [of faith], is resolved through pure faith, is endowed with only the weak degree of the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya), and whose time of birth is not yet fixed.
What is the person who has both accumulated and not yet fully accumulated the provisions?

It is one who, having taken as an object the Dharma dominated by the Truths, has arisen from a middling degree [of application], is resolved through pure faith, is endowed with middling degrees of the factors conducive to liberation, and is certain regarding the time of rebirth.

Who is the person who has accumulated the equipment? It is one who, having taken as an object the Dharma dominated by the Truths, is characterized by a superior degree of resolve, possesses pure faith and resolute conviction, is endowed with the superior factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), and belongs to the period of that very birth.

Furthermore, one who has not yet accumulated the equipment, having taken as an object the Dharma dominated by the truths, is endowed with the mild degree of receptivity (*kṣānti*) that consists in the contemplation of the Dharma of the truths; such a person is endowed with the mild degree of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and is at the stage of a birth from which there is no turning back.

One who has both accumulated and not yet fully accumulated the provisions, having taken as an object the Dharma dominated by truth, is endowed with the receptivity that contemplates the Dharma regarding the truths at a middling degree; such a person, endowed with the middling degrees of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), is one whose birth is certain [to occur] in this very life.

Having accumulated the necessary provisions, having taken as his object the Dharma dominated by the Truths, he is endowed with the superior patience of reflecting upon the Dharma of the Truths, and is endowed with the superior aids to penetration;
this refers to one at the stage of that particular birth.
In that regard, the three levels of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), excluding the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), are momentary by their very nature and non-continuous.

One who attains clear realization at the time of that birth falls away from the previously unobtained stages of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)—whether weak, medium, or intense—as well as from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
And that falling away is due to the falling away of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), but not due to the falling away of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
What is the person who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārī*)?
One who has accumulated the necessary provisions, possesses dull faculties, and applies himself toward the clear realization of the truths by recollecting the instructions of others.

Who is the follower by means of the Dharma (dharmānusārī)? It is one who has accumulated the necessary provisions, possesses sharp faculties, and, having himself recollected the Dharma governed by the Truths, applies himself to the clear realization (abhisamaya) of those Truths.
Who is the one resolved through faith?
It is the person who was a follower by faith at the time of the fruit.
Who is the one who has attained through vision?
It is the person who was a follower of the Dharma at the time of the fruit.
Who is the body-witness?
It is the person who is a learner (śaikṣa) and who practices the eight liberations (vimokṣa).
Who is the one liberated by wisdom? It is that person who has exhausted the outflows and possesses the eight liberations and meditative absorptions.
Who is the one liberated in both ways? It is that person whose outflows are exhausted and who dwells in the eight liberations.
Who is the person practicing for the fruit of stream-entry?
It is that person who exists during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing within the stages conducive to penetration.
Who is the candidate for the stream-entry?
It is that person who exists at the sixteenth moment of mind of the path of seeing.
The path of seeing is the entry into the determination of the truths.
He too, at the time of the clear realization of the Dharma,
being a person who has not yet become free from passion for sensual pleasures, upon entering the fixed course of rightness, becomes a stream-enterer.
One who is largely free from passion, upon entering the fixed course of rightness, becomes a once-returner;
one who is entirely free from passion for sensual desires, upon entering the fixed course of rightness, becomes a non-returner.
When, through the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision, one has entered into the state of stream-entry.
For what reason does one become a stream-enterer through the abandonment of the three fetters?
It is because they comprise the primary [fetters]. On what basis is their primacy established?
On account of being the cause for not setting out;
on account of being the cause for a false departure once one has set out; [and] on account of being the cause for not departing correctly.
And having taken up that [basis].
Furthermore, it is indeed on account of being the cause of error regarding the knowable, the cause of error regarding views, and the cause of error regarding the antidote.
Who is the one practicing for the fruit of once-returning?
It is the person who, on the path of cultivation, is on the path of abandoning the five categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
Who is the once-returner?
It is the person who, on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), is on the path of abandoning the sixth category of afflictions belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara).
Who is the person practicing for the fruit of non-returning?
It is that person who, on the path of cultivation, is on the path of abandoning the seventh and eighth categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
Who is the person who is a non-returner?
It is that person who, on the path of cultivation, is on the path of abandoning the ninth category of afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
When, through the abandonment of all [defilements] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation, one becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī).
For what reason is one called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) due to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
Because they encompass the principal [fetters].
On what basis is its predominance established?
It is established on the basis of being the cause for the lowest state of existence and the cause for the lowest realm.
Who is the person practicing for the fruit of arhatship? It is that person who, on the path of abandoning the eight categories of afflictions belonging to the peak of existence, is still in training.
Who is the Arhat?
It is that person who, on the path of abandoning the ninth category of afflictions belonging to the realm of existence, [attains the fruit].
When, through the abandonment of all afflictions belonging to the three realms and the desire realm, one becomes an Arhat.
For what reason is one called an Arhat due to the abandonment of the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*)?
It is by way of including the principal [fetters]. By including what is the inclusion of the principal?
Based on the fact that it is the cause for grasping at liberation,
and based on the fact that it is the cause for not abandoning what is above,
who is the one for whom seven births at most remain?
A person who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) himself, having transmigrated through existences among gods and humans—whether mixed or unmixed—for seven times at most, attains the end of suffering.
Who is the "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula)? It is one who, having gone from family to family among the gods or among humans, reaches the end of suffering.
Who is the one with one interval?
It is the once-returner who attains the end of suffering among the gods alone.
What is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state? It is one for whom the fetter of rebirth has been abandoned but the fetter of manifestation has not yet been abandoned;

while still bringing forth the intermediate state, such a person either realizes the path and reaches the end of suffering, or, having manifested the intermediate state, proceeds toward the existence of rebirth.
One who, while still intending, brings the path into presence and reaches the end of suffering;
or one who, having formed an intention and set out toward a state of rebirth, brings the path into presence and reaches the end of suffering by means of that very desire for rebirth.
Who is the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth?

It is one for whom both fetters have not yet been abandoned, and who, immediately upon being reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), brings the Path into manifestation and reaches the end of suffering.
Who is the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion?
It is one who, having been reborn, brings the path into manifestation without exertion and reaches the end of suffering.
Who is the one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion?
One who, having been reborn, brings the path into manifestation through exertion and reaches the end of suffering.
Who is the one who flows upwards (ūrdhvaṃstrotas)?

Having been reborn in the realm of form (rūpāvacara), he enters stage by stage as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven; having brought that untainted path (anāsravamārga) into manifestation, he reaches the end of suffering.
Furthermore, another [type] reaches the end of suffering after bringing the path into manifestation as far as the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Furthermore, there are five types of distinctions for the fourth dhyāna when it is cultivated in a mixed manner:
that which is cultivated to a weak degree, cultivated to a medium degree, cultivated to a strong degree, cultivated to a very strong degree, and cultivated to a medium-strong degree.
Through these five distinctions of the fourth dhyāna cultivated in a mixed manner, one is reborn respectively in the five Pure Abodes.
What is an Arhat of the nature of falling away?
One who is of dull faculties by nature, whether distracted or undistracted, and whether intentionally or unintentionally, falls away from the blissful dwelling in the present life.
What is the Arhat of the nature of volition (*cetanādharmā*)?

One who is of dull faculties by nature, whether distracted or undistracted, falls away from the dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) without intending to do so, but does not fall away when intending to do so.
What is the Arhat of the nature of guarding?
One who is of dull faculties by nature, when distracted, falls away from the pleasant dwelling in the present life; when undistracted, he does not fall away.
What is the Arhat who is steadfast and unshakable?
He is one whose nature is of dull faculties, who, whether distracted or undistracted, neither falls away from the dwelling in happiness in this very life nor sharpens his faculties.
What is the Arhat of the nature of penetration (*prativedhanā-dharman*)?

One who is of dull faculties by nature, whether distracted or undistracted, does not fall away from dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*), but merely sharpens his faculties.
Who is the Arhat of immovable nature?
One who is by nature of sharp faculties, whether distracted or undistracted, does not undergo falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Who is the ordinary person belonging to the desire realm?
It is a person who has been born in the desire realm and has not attained the state of a noble one.

Who is the learner (śaikṣa) belonging to the desire realm? It is a person who has been born in the desire realm and has attained the state of a learner, yet for whom some fetters (saṃyojana) still remain.
Who is the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) belonging to the desire realm?
It is a person who has been reborn in the desire realm and has attained the noble Dharma,
such that no fetter remains.
Just as there are three belonging to the desire realm, so too there are those belonging to the form realm and the formless realm.

Who is the bodhisattva belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) and the form realm (rūpāvacara)? It is a person who, being endowed with meditative absorption (dhyāna) that is withdrawn from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), dwells in the pleasures of dhyāna; such a person is reborn both in the desire realm and in the form realm. Who is the pratyekabuddha belonging to the desire realm? [It is one who is reborn in the desire realm.]
In an era devoid of Buddhas, within the desire realm, he personally realized the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.

Who is the person that is a bodhisattva practicing with resolute intention?
It is the bodhisattva who is established in the ten stages.
Who is the person that is a bodhisattva practicing with signs?
It is the bodhisattva who is established in the stages of Pramuditā, Vimalā, Prabhākari, Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, and Abhimukhī.

Who is the person that is a bodhisattva practicing without volitional effort?
It is the bodhisattva who is established in the stages (bhūmis) of Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā.
Furthermore, the person who is called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is of two types:
one who attains liberation gradually (krama-nairyāṇika) and one who attains liberation all at once (sakṛt-nairyāṇika).
The one who attains liberation gradually is as previously described.

One who is "liberated by a single means" (sakṛnnairyāṇika), having entered into the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) and relying upon an attainment not yet reached, abandons all afflictions belonging to the three realms simultaneously by means of the supramundane path he has realized; he abandons them according to their types. He is designated as being in two of the fruits: the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
Furthermore, that person attains full realization (ājñā) either in this very life at the time of death;
or, if they do not attain it, then by the power of their aspiration,
having been reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) during a period when no Buddha has appeared, they become a Pratyekabuddha.
